Question 124 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (C) Steric constraints are relaxed at the 3' position of the mRNA codon (and the complementary 5' first position of the tRNA anticodon...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Codon-anticodon geometry: A codon is read 5' → 3' on mRNA, and pairs in an antiparallel orientation with the tRNA anticodon (read 3' → 5'). The first two positions of the codon pair with the third and second positions of the anticodon via strict, canonical Watson-Crick rules (A-U and G-C).
  • Step 2: The wobble position: The third nucleotide of the codon (at the 3' end) pairs with the first nucleotide of the anticodon (at the 5' end). Francis Crick showed that the spatial geometry of the ribosomal decoding center at this third position permits flexible, non-standard ('wobble') spatial conformations.
  • Step 3: Wobble rules and inosine: For instance, a 5'-G on the anticodon can form stable hydrogen bonds with either a 3'-C or a 3'-U on the mRNA codon. Furthermore, post-transcriptional modification of adenine by tRNA-specific deaminase generates the purine base Inosine (I). An anticodon possessing 5'-Inosine can base-pair with three distinct synonymous codons ending in U, C, or A. This enables ~45 distinct tRNAs to decode all 61 sense codons accurately without compromising translational fidelity.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) a tRNA's amino acid is attached covalently by its specific aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and cannot change identities.
  • ✗ (B) the genetic code is strictly triplet; skipping bases causes catastrophic frameshift mutations.
  • ✗ (D) codons utilize all four bases (A, U, G, C) across all three positions.
Question 125 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (B) They employ a two-step 'double-sieve' mechanism: an activation active site admits the correct amino acid (and similarly sized inco...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: The fidelity challenge: Several amino acids have nearly identical structures. For example, isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase must distinguish isoleucine from valine, which differs by only a single methyl group (-CH2-). Valine is slightly smaller than isoleucine and can fit into the synthetic active site ~1% of the time, which would result in unacceptably high error rates.
  • Step 2: The double-sieve mechanism (Alan Fersht model): Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases utilize two distinct catalytic pockets: 1) Synthetic sieve: Excludes amino acids that are too large to fit into the activation cleft. Isoleucine and valine are both activated with ATP to form aminoacyl-AMP. 2) Editing/hydrolytic sieve: This separate cleft is smaller than the synthetic site. Isoleucine is too large to enter the editing cleft and is preserved. However, incorrectly activated valyl-AMP (or valyl-tRNAᴵˡᵉ) enters the editing pocket, where it is immediately hydrolyzed into free valine and AMP.
  • Step 3: Outcome: This proofreading mechanism drops the net error rate of aminoacylation to less than 1 mistake per 10,000 to 50,000 reactions, ensuring high fidelity in cellular protein synthesis.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) aaRS enzymes edit mischarged tRNAs locally; they do not destroy the entire ribosome.
  • ✗ (C) tRNA aminoacylation is extraordinarily specific; random charging would produce completely scrambled, non-functional proteomes.
  • ✗ (D) reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA, playing no role in tRNA charging.
Question 126 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (D) 1) Elongation factor EF-Tu (or eEF1A) delivers the cognate aminoacyl-tRNA to the A (aminoacyl) site in a GTP-dependent step; 2) Th...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Aminoacyl-tRNA delivery to A site: The ternary complex consisting of elongation factor EF-Tu, GTP, and charged aminoacyl-tRNA enters the ribosomal A site. If anticodon-codon pairing matches, GTP is hydrolyzed, EF-Tu-GDP dissociates, and the aminoacyl-tRNA accommodates fully into the peptidyl transferase center.
  • Step 2: Peptidyl transferase reaction: The nucleophilic alpha-amino group of the A-site amino acid attacks the high-energy ester carbon linking the growing polypeptide chain to the P-site tRNA. Crucially, crystal structures by Thomas Steitz revealed that the catalytic center consists purely of RNA nucleotides from the large ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA in bacteria, 28S rRNA in eukaryotes) with no protein within 18 Å of the active site. Thus, the ribosome is fundamentally a catalytic ribozyme.
  • Step 3: Translocation: Elongation factor EF-G (eEF2 in eukaryotes) binds to the ribosome and hydrolyzes GTP, inducing a massive structural ratchet rotation. The ribosome advances exactly one codon (3 nucleotides) toward the 3' end of the mRNA. The uncharged tRNA moves from P to E (exit) site and diffuses away, while the new peptidyl-tRNA moves from A to P site. The A site is now vacant and positioned over the next codon.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) incoming tRNAs enter the A site, not the E site, and mRNA is not degraded during elongation.
  • ✗ (B) ATP synthase does not function inside the ribosome; elongation is driven by GTPase factors EF-Tu and EF-G.
  • ✗ (C) peptide bonds form in the A site, and uncharged tRNAs exit via the E site, not the polypeptide chain.

HDACs remove acetyl groups from histones, restoring positive charges, compacting chromatin into dense heterochromatin, and stably silencing gene expression.

  • ✗ (C) tRNAs carry amino acids, whereas miRNAs are regulatory non-coding RNAs that do not carry amino acids or glucose.
  • ✗ (D) miRNAs do not coat nuclear pores; they bind specific cytosolic mRNAs.
Question 134 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (B) Nonsense mutation: changes a sense codon into one of the three translation termination codons (UAA, UAG, or UGA), resulting in pre...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Definitions of point mutations: Point mutations can be classified into three primary categories depending on their impact on translation: silent, missense, and nonsense.
  • Step 2: Nonsense mutation analysis: A nonsense mutation occurs when a single nucleotide substitution transforms an amino acid-specifying (sense) codon into an in-frame stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA). When the translating ribosome encounters this premature stop codon, release factors bind immediately, terminating elongation prematurely. The resulting truncated protein almost always loses catalytic activity and is often degraded by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
  • Step 3: Other mutation types: 1) Silent (synonymous) mutation: Changes a codon to a synonymous codon (e.g., GAG to GAA, both encoding glutamic acid due to genetic code degeneracy), resulting in zero change to the primary amino acid sequence. 2) Missense mutation: Changes a codon so that it encodes a different amino acid (e.g., GAG [Glu] to GUG [Val] in sickle cell anemia).
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) changing an amino acid codon into a stop codon is a nonsense mutation, not a silent mutation.
  • ✗ (C) a mutation that leaves the amino acid sequence unchanged is a silent mutation, whereas a missense mutation substitutes a different amino acid.
  • ✗ (D) a frameshift mutation is caused by insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of 3, shifting the entire downstream triplet reading frame.
Question 135 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (C) Because the genetic code is read in non-overlapping nucleotide triplets, deleting 1 base pair alters the triplet reading frame for...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: The triplet reading frame: During translation, the ribosome establishes a strict reading frame starting from the initiator AUG codon, advancing precisely 3 nucleotides (one codon) at each elongation step.
  • Step 2: Mechanism of frameshift mutations: Inserting or deleting any number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of 3 (e.g., +1, -1, +2, -2) alters the grouping of all downstream nucleotides. Every single codon downstream of the mutation is misread into an incorrect amino acid, completely scrambling the primary structure of the protein. Furthermore, because stop codons occur randomly ~3/64 times in non-coding sequences, frameshifted reading frames almost always encounter an out-of-frame stop codon within a few dozen codons, yielding a severely truncated, misfolded, and non-functional protein.
  • Step 3: In-frame 3-bp indels: A 3-bp deletion (such as the classic DeltaF508 mutation in CFTR, which deletes three nucleotides CTT, removing a single phenylalanine at position 508) eliminates exactly one codon while keeping the remaining hundreds of downstream codons in their proper reading frame. Although the loss of a single amino acid can cause misfolding, it preserves the remainder of the protein sequence.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) nuclear genes frequently suffer both 1-bp and 3-bp indels; deletions do not target membranes.
  • ✗ (B) primase synthesizes RNA primers in replication and cannot repair deletions in genomic DNA.
  • ✗ (D) the ribosome cannot guess or compensate for missing nucleotides, strictly decoding what is presented.

Question 136 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (D) Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER); a multiprotein repair complex recognizes the helical distortion, an excinuclease endonucleolytic...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Lesion nature: UV radiation (specifically UV-B ~290-320 nm) excites adjacent thymine or cytosine rings, inducing [2+2] cycloaddition to form cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) or 6-4 photoproducts. These bulky lesions create a ~30° bend and distort the regular B-DNA helical geometry, completely arresting replicative DNA polymerases during S phase.
  • Step 2: Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) mechanism: 1) Recognition: In humans, XPC-RAD23B detects the helical distortion (global genome NER), or stalled RNA Polymerase II recruits CSA and CSB (transcription-coupled NER). 2) Dual incision: TFIIH helicases (XPB/XPD) unwind the local DNA around the lesion (~30 bp). Dual endonucleases XPF and XPG introduce phosphodiester incisions on either side of the dimer (5' and 3' incisions). 3) Excision: The ~24-32 nucleotide lesion-containing oligomer is excised and released. 4) Resynthesis and ligation: DNA Polymerase delta/epsilon resynthesizes the missing patch using the undamaged complementary strand as a template, and DNA Ligase I or Ligase III-XRCC1 seals the final phosphodiester nick.
  • Step 3: Clinical disease: Individuals with Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) harbor autosomal recessive loss-of-function mutations in XP repair genes (XPA-XPG). Lacking functional NER, unrepaired pyrimidine dimers lead to replication fork collapse and high rates of C→T transition mutations, resulting in severe solar keratosis and a thousand-fold spike in cutaneous melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) MMR corrects non-bulky replication mismatches (e.g., A paired with C), and defects cause Lynch syndrome (HNPCC), not Huntington's.
  • ✗ (B) homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks, not bulky pyrimidine dimers.
  • ✗ (C) placental mammals lack photolyase enzymes (which utilize blue light for direct photoreactivation) and rely exclusively on NER.
Question 137 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) DNA fragments migrate toward the positive electrode (anode) because the sugar-phosphate backbone carries a constant negative charg...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Net electrical charge of DNA: At physiological and alkaline buffer pH (such as TAE buffer, pH 8.0), each phosphodiester linkage along the DNA sugar-phosphate backbone contains a fully deprotonated phosphate group bearing a negative charge (-1). Because there is one negative charge per nucleotide, DNA has a uniform charge-to-mass ratio regardless of sequence or length.
  • Step 2: Direction of migration: In an electric field, negatively charged anions migrate toward the positively charged electrode (the anode, typically colored red).
  • Step 3: Molecular sieving through the agarose matrix: Agarose forms a three-dimensional cross-linked polymer mesh with microscopic pores. Large DNA molecules encounter substantial frictional resistance and drag as they thread through the pores (reptation model), impeding their progress. Shorter, compact DNA fragments snake through the pores with minimal hindrance. Consequently, smaller fragments migrate much faster and travel significantly farther during a fixed time run. The distance migrated is inversely proportional to the log10 of the fragment length in base pairs (bp).
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) DNA is negatively charged and migrates toward the positive anode (not negative cathode), and smaller fragments migrate faster (not larger ones).
  • ✗ (C) electrophoresis is an active migration process through buffer without boiling or destroying the gel.
  • ✗ (D) migration distance is determined by molecular size/length through the sieving gel pores, not atomic ratios.
Question 138 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (C) Step 1 (Denaturation, ~95°C): High thermal kinetic energy breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary strands, melting the double-...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Denaturation (~94-96°C): High thermal energy disrupts the non-covalent hydrogen bonds holding complementary base pairs together without breaking covalent phosphodiester bonds, yielding two separated single-stranded DNA templates.
  • Step 2: Annealing (~50-65°C): The temperature is lowered to a point calculated from the melting temperature (Tm) of the primers. Primers are present in vast molar excess (>100,000-fold) over template DNA, so primer-template hybridization is kinetically favored over template-template reannealing. The forward and reverse primers anneal specifically to complementary sequences flanking the target sequence on opposite strands.
  • Step 3: Extension (~72°C): The thermal cycler heats to the optimal catalytic temperature for Taq DNA polymerase (~72°C). Taq extends the primers from their 3'-OH ends by incorporating complementary dNTPs at a rate of ~1,000 nucleotides per minute. Each cycle doubles the target sequence (2ⁿ amplification), producing ~1 billion copies in 30 cycles.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) PCR relies on automated thermal cycling of DNA replication, not boiling destruction and freezing crystallization.
  • ✗ (B) this scrambles the temperature sequence and misidentifies the biochemical processes.
  • ✗ (D) PCR does not require helicase (heat denatures DNA), RNA polymerase, or ribosomes.

  • Step 1: Palindromic recognition sequences: Type II restriction endonucleases recognize symmetric palindromic sequences that read identically 5' → 3' on both strands (e.g., 5'-GAATTC-3' on the top strand and 3'-CTTAAG-5' on the bottom strand).
  • Step 2: Generation of sticky ends: EcoRI cleaves the phosphodiester backbone between the G and the first A on both antiparallel strands. Because the cleavage sites are offset by 4 base pairs, the enzyme leaves protruding 4-nucleotide 5' single-stranded extensions (5'-AATT-3') known as cohesive or 'sticky' ends.
  • Step 3: Recombinant annealing and ligation: Because both the cloning plasmid and the cDNA insert were digested with the identical restriction enzyme (EcoRI), their sticky ends are perfectly complementary. In solution, the overhangs readily base-pair via transient hydrogen bonds. T4 DNA Ligase is then added with ATP to catalyze the formation of covalent phosphodiester bonds between the 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate termini, permanently joining the foreign cDNA insert into the circular plasmid vector to create a recombinant molecule.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) EcoRI produces cohesive 5' sticky ends, not blunt ends, and autoclaving at 200°C would denature and destroy DNA.
  • ✗ (C) alkaline phosphatase removes phosphate groups (not restriction enzymes), and ligation requires covalent phosphodiester bonds.
  • ✗ (D) plasmids are non-viral circular extrachromosomal DNA, not infectious retroviruses.
Question 140 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (D) Ampicillin is a beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits transpeptidase enzymes required for bacterial peptidoglycan cell wall cross-l...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Mechanism of transformation: Bacterial transformation is the process by which competent bacterial cells take up foreign naked DNA from their extracellular environment. Chemical competence with calcium chloride neutralizes the negative charges on DNA and phospholipid lipopolysaccharides, and a brief heat shock (42°C for 45 seconds) creates transient pores in the bacterial cell membrane through which plasmid DNA enters.
  • Step 2: Low transformation efficiency: In typical laboratory protocols, fewer than 1 in 10,000 bacterial cells successfully take up a plasmid. Therefore, a powerful selective screen is required to eliminate the vast sea of untransformed cells.
  • Step 3: Antibiotic selection: Ampicillin inhibits bacterial transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins), preventing the formation of peptide cross-links in the peptidoglycan cell wall. As dividing bacteria attempt to synthesize new cell walls, osmotic pressure causes them to swell, rupture, and lyse.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) ampicillin is a bactericidal antibiotic, not a nutrient or metabolic sugar.
  • ✗ (B) bacteria do not commit voluntary apoptosis to yield space for plasmids; untransformed cells die from osmotic lysis.
  • ✗ (C) heat shock is merely a physical method to permeabilize membranes and does not confer antibiotic resistance without plasmid uptake.
Question 141 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) A synthetic single-guide RNA (sgRNA) contains a 20-nucleotide guide sequence complementary to the target genomic DNA; Cas9 scans t...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Mechanism of target recognition: The engineered CRISPR-Cas9 tool utilizes two components: the Cas9 endonuclease protein (from Streptococcus pyogenes) and a single-guide RNA (sgRNA, fusing crRNA and tracrRNA). The 5' end of the sgRNA contains 20 nucleotides designed to be complementary to the target chromosomal DNA sequence.
  • Step 2: PAM requirement and cleavage: Before unwinding the DNA, Cas9 must first bind a conserved Protospacer Adjacent Motif (PAM), which is 5'-NGG-3' on the non-target strand. PAM recognition triggers local double-helix melting, allowing the sgRNA to base-pair with the complementary target strand. Cas9's two distinct catalytic nuclease domains—HNH (cleaving the target strand) and RuvC (cleaving the non-target strand)—generate a blunt double-strand break (DSB) precisely 3 base pairs upstream of the PAM.
  • Step 3: Repair pathways and knockout: Eukaryotic cells repair double-strand breaks through one of two pathways: 1) Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ): An error-prone repair mechanism that rejoins the blunt ends without a template. NHEJ frequently introduces random insertions or deletions (indels) of 1-10 base pairs. In a protein-coding exon, these indels cause frameshift mutations, producing premature stop codons and functional gene knockout. 2) Homology-Directed Repair (HDR): If an exogenous donor DNA template with homologous flanking arms is co-introduced, the cell uses HDR to achieve precise gene knock-in or correction.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) Cas9 is a targeted sequence-specific endonuclease guided by RNA, not an antibody destroying cell walls.
  • ✗ (C) Cas9 cleaves the phosphodiester backbone, not converting thymines to uracils or creating retroviruses.
  • ✗ (D) Cas9 is an endonuclease that cuts DNA, not a ligase adding telomeres.

Question 142 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (D) ddNTPs lack a hydroxyl group (-OH) at both the 2' and 3' carbon positions of the pentose sugar ring (possessing only hydrogen atom...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Chemical structure of dNTP vs ddNTP: Standard 2'-deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) lack an -OH at the 2' carbon (having an -H instead), but retain an active hydroxyl group (-OH) at the 3' carbon position of the ribose ring.
  • Step 2: Chain-termination mechanism: Dideoxynucleoside triphosphates (ddNTPs) lack the hydroxyl group at BOTH the 2' and 3' carbons (hence 'dideoxy'). When DNA polymerase incorporates a ddNTP into a growing DNA chain, the lack of a 3'-OH group means there is no nucleophile available to react with the 5'-triphosphate of the next incoming dNTP. Consequently, phosphodiester bond formation cannot occur, and chain extension is permanently terminated at that exact base position.
  • Step 3: Detection: In modern automated Sanger sequencing, four distinct fluorescent dye terminators (each emitting light at a characteristic wavelength for ddATP, ddTTP, ddCTP, and ddGTP) are included at low concentrations along with normal dNTPs. This generates a nested set of truncated fragments representing every nucleotide position. Capillary gel electrophoresis separates these fragments by single-base resolution, and a laser optical detector reads the terminal fluorescent signal, outputting the sequence chromatogram in the 5' → 3' direction.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) ddNTPs possess normal nitrogenous bases (A, T, C, G) that form complementary hydrogen bonds perfectly.
  • ✗ (B) ddNTPs possess standard triphosphate groups (three phosphates), not four.
  • ✗ (C) ddNTPs are nucleotides joined by phosphodiester bonds, containing zero peptide bonds.
Question 143 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) Bacterial cells lack spliceosomes and small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs); prokaryotes cannot excise eukaryotic non-coding i...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Structural differences in eukaryotic vs prokaryotic gene architecture: Eukaryotic protein-coding genes are interrupted by non-coding intervening sequences (introns) interspersed between coding sequences (exons). Human genes often contain 90-95% intron sequence.
  • Step 2: Prokaryotic transcriptional machinery: Bacteria do not possess introns in their protein-coding genes and completely lack the complex splicing machinery (the spliceosome, snRNAs, and associated splicing factors) needed to recognize and excise eukaryotic introns.
  • Step 3: The cDNA solution: If an intact human genomic gene with introns is placed behind a bacterial promoter, bacterial RNA polymerase will transcribe a polycistronic mRNA containing both exons and introns. The bacterial ribosome will attempt to translate this unprocessed transcript directly, encountering out-of-frame stop codons and nonsense sequences within the introns, resulting in an inactive, truncated, misfolded polypeptide.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) human DNA is composed of standard organic nucleotides, not toxic heavy metals, and bacteria lack mitochondria.
  • ✗ (C) the triplet genetic code (3 bases per codon) is universally conserved across all domains of life.
  • ✗ (D) reverse transcriptase synthesizes DNA from an RNA template, not RNA from DNA.
Question 144 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (C) The specific gene represented by that spot is transcribed at significantly higher levels (upregulated/overexpressed) in the gliobl...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Principles of two-color DNA microarrays: A DNA microarray consists of a solid substrate (glass slide or silicon chip) displaying an organized microscopic grid of thousands of distinct single-stranded DNA oligonucleotide probes, each corresponding to a known gene.
  • Step 2: Competitive hybridization: mRNAs from experimental (cancer, labeled with Cy5, red) and control (normal, labeled with Cy3, green) tissues are reverse-transcribed into fluorescently labeled cDNAs, mixed in equal quantities, and allowed to hybridize competitively to complementary probes on the chip.
  • Step 3: Signal interpretation: 1) Yellow spot: Equal hybridization of red and green cDNAs indicates equal gene expression in both tissues. 2) Green spot: Predominance of green cDNA indicates the gene is downregulated or silenced in tumor cells. 3) Red spot: High abundance of red cDNA indicates that transcripts for that gene are present in vastly higher quantities in the cancer cells compared to normal tissue (overexpression/upregulation). For instance, genes encoding EGFR or telomerase typically light up bright red in glioblastoma profiling.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) a deleted gene would produce zero mRNA and appear dark/black, not bright red.
  • ✗ (B) equal expression produces a blended yellow fluorescence (red + green = yellow).
  • ✗ (D) red fluorescence comes from synthetic fluorescent Cy5-dUTP dyes incorporated into human cDNA, not bacterial chlorophyll.

Question 145 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (B) Natural selection does not create new phenotypic traits in response to environmental need; instead, heritable variation arises spo...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Lamarck's mechanism: Lamarck hypothesized use and disuse (body structures develop with use and atrophy with disuse) and the inheritance of acquired traits (changes acquired by an individual during its lifetime are transmitted to offspring). However, somatic changes acquired during life (e.g., muscle hypertrophy or stretched necks) do not alter the nucleotide sequence of germline gametes.
  • Step 2: Darwinian natural selection: Natural selection operates on pre-existing heritable genetic variation already present in the gene pool. Mutations arise randomly with respect to the organism's needs; the environment does not direct which mutations occur. Instead, the environment acts as a passive selective filter.
  • Step 3: Differential reproductive success: In ancestral giraffe populations, individuals that randomly inherited alleles conferring slightly longer cervical vertebrae could forage on higher acacia canopy browse that competitors could not reach. Better nutrition led to higher survival, lower infant mortality, and greater fecundity (differential reproductive fitness). Over many generations, the frequency of alleles conferring longer necks increased in the population gene pool.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) mutations are random and organisms cannot voluntarily choose or direct their mutations.
  • ✗ (C) somatic exercise or physiological adaptation does not rewrite germline DNA sequences.
  • ✗ (D) natural selection operates autonomously in all wild biological populations without human intervention.
Question 146 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (D) Pre-existing, rare genetic variants in the bacterial population possessed mutations (such as the mecA gene encoding an altered pen...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Clarification of evolutionary misconception: Antibiotics DO NOT cause or induce resistance mutations. Antibiotics are antimicrobial chemicals, not directed mutagens that instruct bacteria how to survive.
  • Step 2: Pre-existing variation: In massive bacterial populations (billions of cells with rapid doubling times), spontaneous replication errors and horizontal gene transfer (conjugation, transduction, transformation) generate vast genetic diversity. Rare bacterial individuals already carried the mecA gene, which encodes an alternative transpeptidase enzyme (penicillin-binding protein 2a, PBP2a) with low binding affinity for beta-lactams.
  • Step 3: Differential survival under selective pressure: In the absence of methicillin, resistant strains may have had no selective advantage (or even a slight metabolic fitness cost). However, widespread clinical administration of methicillin killed off nearly all competing susceptible bacteria. The rare mecA-carrying MRSA cells survived this intense selective bottleneck, reproduced without competition for nutrients, and passed the resistance determinant to all clonal descendants. Consequently, the population allele frequency of mecA increased dramatically over time.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) antibiotics act as selective agents, not directed mutagens that cause resistant mutations.
  • ✗ (B) bacteria do not 'learn' or voluntarily alter their metabolism to eat antibiotics.
  • ✗ (C) the host immune system attempts to clear the bacteria; resistance is mediated by bacterial enzymes, not patient antibodies.
Question 147 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (C) Industrial coal pollution killed the sensitive lichens and darkened tree trunks with soot; on the blackened bark, light moths were...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Ecological shift: Before industrialization, rural English woodlands featured tree trunks covered in pale, epiphytic lichens. The light, mottled morph of Biston betularia blended in against this background, escaping detection by visual avian predators (such as robins and thrushes). The dark melanic morph stood out sharply against pale bark and was heavily predated.
  • Step 2: Industrial pollution: With the rise of the Industrial Revolution, heavy sulfur dioxide emissions killed off the lichens, and airborne soot coated tree bark in dark grime.
  • Step 3: Reversal of selective advantage: On the soot-darkened trunks, the selective pressures reversed completely. The light moths were conspicuous and suffered heavy mortality from bird predation. The dark morph (carbonaria, caused by a transposable element insertion in the cortex gene) enjoyed cryptic camouflage, experiencing significantly higher survival rates and leaving more offspring.

  • ✗ (A) coal smoke does not mutate moths into birds; moths and birds belong to different phyla.

★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (B) A small, unassuming male songbird that lives for only 3 years, but successfully defends a nest territory, mates with two females, ...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Scientific definition of Darwinian fitness: In evolutionary biology, fitness (denoted as w) is defined strictly as an individual's relative genetic contribution to the gene pool of the next generation—measured by the number of viable, fertile offspring that survive to reproductive age.
  • Step 2: Analysis of options: 1) The bull elk in (A) has high physical strength and long lifespan, but produces zero offspring (fitness = 0). 2) The songbird in (B) has a modest lifespan of only 3 years, but produces 14 fertile offspring that reach adulthood and transmit its genes into future generations (fitness > 0). 3) The sea turtle in (C) and cedar tree in (D) possess impressive physiological adaptations, but leave zero surviving descendants (fitness = 0).
  • Step 3: Core conclusion: Evolution does not reward physical strength, speed, or longevity in isolation; these traits matter only to the extent that they enhance an organism's relative reproductive success (passing alleles to the next generation).
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) sterile individuals leave zero genes to subsequent generations (fitness = 0).
  • ✗ (C) producing zero surviving offspring results in zero genetic representation in the next generation.
  • ✗ (D) living 500 years without producing viable seeds yields zero evolutionary fitness.
Question 149 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) Heterozygote advantage (balancing selection); heterozygous individuals (HbA/HbS, sickle-cell trait) exhibit increased resistance t...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Genotypes and fitness in malaria-endemic zones: In sub-Saharan Africa, Plasmodium falciparum malaria is a major cause of childhood mortality. The population consists of three genotypes at the beta-globin locus: 1) HbA/HbA (homozygous wild-type): Normal red blood cells, but highly susceptible to severe, lethal cerebral malaria (lower fitness). 2) HbS/HbS (homozygous mutant): Severe sickle cell disease, high childhood mortality in historical contexts (low fitness). 3) HbA/HbS (heterozygous): Sickle cell trait. Their red blood cells have normal morphology under normal oxygen tensions, but when infected by Plasmodium, parasitized erythrocytes sickle prematurely and are destroyed by the spleen, limiting parasite replication and conferring ~80-90% protection against lethal severe malaria.
  • Step 2: Concept of heterozygote advantage: Because the heterozygote (HbA/HbS) has a higher Darwinian fitness than either homozygote (HbA/HbA or HbS/HbS) in environments where malaria is prevalent, natural selection actively preserves both alleles.
  • Step 3: Balanced polymorphism: Mating between two heterozygotes (HbA/HbS × HbA/HbS) will continually produce all three genotypes in a 1:2:1 ratio each generation, ensuring the persistence of the deleterious HbS allele at a stable equilibrium frequency. When descendants migrate to malaria-free regions (such as North America), the selective advantage disappears, and the frequency of HbS gradually declines due to purifying selection against HbS/HbS.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) sickle cell anemia is a hereditary genetic disorder caused by a missense mutation (Glu6Val), not dietary salt intake.
  • ✗ (C) HbS is recessive for severe sickle cell disease, not dominant.
  • ✗ (D) mosquitoes are biological vectors transmitting the eukaryotic parasite Plasmodium, not injecting globin genes into human genomes.

Question 151 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) Directional selection shifts the overall population phenotypic mean toward one extreme phenotype (e.g., larger beak depth in Galáp...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Directional selection: Operates when environmental conditions favor individuals exhibiting phenotypes at one end of the phenotypic distribution. Peter and Rosemary Grant observed this in Geospiza fortis on Daphne Major: severe drought eliminated small soft seeds, leaving large tough seeds. Birds with deeper beaks could crack these tough seeds, shifting the average beak depth of the surviving population to the right (higher mean).
  • Step 2: Stabilizing selection: Acts against extreme phenotypes and favors the intermediate phenotypic optimum. In humans, infant mortality is significantly higher for very low birth weight babies (due to immature organ systems) and very high birth weight babies (due to maternal pelvic complications during birth). Consequently, natural selection maintains birth weights centered near 3.5 kg, reducing phenotypic variance without shifting the mean.
  • Step 3: Disruptive (diversifying) selection: Occurs when environmental conditions favor individuals at both extremes of the phenotypic spectrum over intermediate phenotypes. In the black-bellied seedcracker (Pyrenestes ostrinus), birds feed on two distinct sedge species: one producing hard seeds (cracked only by very large beaks) and one producing soft seeds (efficiently handled by small beaks). Intermediate beaks are inefficient at handling both seed types, producing a bimodal distribution.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) selection alters survival and reproductive rates of existing phenotypes, not directly doubling mutation rates or converting all animals to herbivores.
  • ✗ (C) directional selection actively changes allele frequencies toward favored extremes.
  • ✗ (D) all three modes of selection operate universally across animals, plants, fungi, and microbes.
Question 152 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (C) A severe population bottleneck; dramatic reduction of population size drastically amplified genetic drift, causing random fixation...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Population bottleneck definition: A population bottleneck occurs when a catastrophic event (e.g., overhunting, habitat destruction, disease epidemic, volcanic eruption) drastically reduces population size to a small fraction of its original numbers.
  • Step 2: Mechanism of genetic drift: In small populations, random sampling error (genetic drift) overwhelms natural selection. By sheer chance, many rare and moderately common alleles present in the ancestral population were not carried by the ~20-30 surviving seals and were permanently lost from the species' gene pool.
  • Step 3: Allele fixation and demographic rebound: Many remaining loci drifted to complete fixation (100% homozygosity). Although the census population size (N) rebounded to >200,000 seals through exponential reproduction, all modern individuals are descended from that tiny founder gene pool. Recovery of genetic diversity requires tens of thousands of generations of new de novo mutations, leaving the species vulnerable to emerging pathogens and environmental shifts.

  • ✗ (B) hunting was physical (harpoons/rifles), not mutagens altering DNA polymerase fidelity.
  • ✗ (D) meiosis and crossing over continue normally; the lack of diversity stems from alleles being identical across homologues.

Question 154 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (B) It reduces genetic differences and allele frequency divergence between the two populations, tending to homogenize their gene pools...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Definition of gene flow: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations resulting from migration of individuals or dispersal of gametes (e.g., pollen drifting between plant patches, juvenile wolves dispersing between packs).
  • Step 2: Homogenizing effect: When two populations exchange migrants at a high rate, new alleles entering each population are mixed into the local gene pool. This continuous genetic exchange counteracts the divergent effects of local natural selection and genetic drift.
  • Step 3: Impact on speciation: High gene flow keeps the two populations genetically similar (homogenization), maintaining them as a single cohesive evolutionary lineage. For speciation to occur, gene flow must be restricted or severed (e.g., by geographic barriers or reproductive isolation) to allow evolutionary forces to drive genetic divergence.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) high gene flow prevents (rather than accelerates) speciation by eliminating genetic differences between populations.
  • ✗ (C) polyploidy arises from meiotic non-disjunction or hybridization, not from migration of individuals.
  • ✗ (D) gene flow mixes existing alleles; it does not stop baseline spontaneous mutation rates.
Question 155 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (C) It defines the precise non-evolving baseline conditions (no mutation, random mating, no gene flow, infinitely large population siz...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Role of a null hypothesis in science: A null hypothesis describes what would be observed if NO experimental effect, change, or process were taking place.
  • Step 2: The five Hardy-Weinberg assumptions: A population's gene pool remains in strict equilibrium (frequencies of alleles p and q, and genotypes p², 2pq, q² stay constant across generations) ONLY if all five conditions are met simultaneously: 1) No mutations (no new alleles introduced), 2) Random mating (no sexual selection or assortative mating), 3) No gene flow (no migration into or out of the population), 4) Extremely large population size (no genetic drift / sampling error), 5) No natural selection (all genotypes have equal survival and reproductive fitness).
  • Step 3: Evolutionary testing: In nature, virtually no wild population satisfies all five conditions indefinitely. Therefore, Hardy-Weinberg serves as a benchmark model. By comparing observed empirical genotype frequencies to calculated Hardy-Weinberg expected frequencies using a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, biologists can detect statistically significant departures, pinpointing which evolutionary mechanisms (e.g., selection or non-random mating) are driving microevolution at that specific locus.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) real wild populations virtually never satisfy all five conditions simultaneously.
  • ✗ (B) Hardy-Weinberg demonstrates how and when evolution does occur by highlighting deviations from equilibrium.
  • ✗ (D) Hardy-Weinberg analyzes population allele frequencies, not radioactive isotope decay in fossils.
Question 156 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (D) Approximately 0.0198 (~2.0% of the population, or roughly 1 in 50 individuals)
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Identify given frequency: Individuals with PKU are homozygous recessive (genotype aa). Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of homozygous recessive individuals is given by q²: q² = 1 / 10,000 = 0.0001.
  • Step 2: Calculate recessive allele frequency (q): q = √(q²) = √(0.0001) = 0.01.
  • Step 3: Calculate dominant allele frequency (p): Because p + q = 1: p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.01 = 0.99.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) 0.0001 is q² (the affected homozygous recessive frequency), not the carrier frequency 2pq.
  • ✗ (B) 0.001 is an arithmetic calculation error.
  • ✗ (C) a carrier frequency of 50% would require allele frequencies of p = 0.5 and q = 0.5 (where 25% of the population would have PKU).

STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION

  • Step 2: Analogous structures and convergent evolution: Analogous features share similar biological functions and superficial appearances, but do NOT share a common ancestral origin for that trait. Instead, they arise independently through convergent evolution when unrelated lineages adapt to similar ecological niches or physical challenges. A bird wing (modified tetrapod forelimb composed of bones and feathers) and an insect wing (chitinous outfolding of the thoracic exoskeleton) are analogous: both generate aerodynamic lift, but their common ancestor had no wings.

  • Step 1: Universal molecular homology: The strongest evidence for the universal common ancestry of all terrestrial life (LUCA) comes from molecular biology. Despite immense macroscopic diversity across billions of species, the internal molecular operating system of life is universally conserved.
  • Step 2: Key conserved molecular features: 1) Universal genetic code: The codon 5'-AUG-3' specifies methionine, 5'-UGG-3' specifies tryptophan, and 5'-UAA-3' signals stop across bacteria, plants, and humans.   • Step 3: Evolutionary conclusion: There is no physical or chemical reason why life could not utilize a 4-base codon, alternative non-canonical amino acids, or alternative nucleoside triphosphates (e.g., GTP or CTP) as the universal energy currency. The fact that all extant life shares these specific arbitrary biochemical features proves that they were inherited from a single common ancestral lineage that evolved over 3.8 billion years ago.

Question 161 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (B) Relatedness between two taxa is determined strictly by the recency of their Most Recent Common Ancestor (MRCA), represented by the...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Reading tree topology: In phylogenetic systematics, trees represent hypotheses of evolutionary descent. Branching points (nodes) represent the Most Recent Common Ancestor (MRCA) of the descendant lineages.
  • Step 2: Determining evolutionary kinship: Taxon A is more closely related to Taxon B than to Taxon C if and only if Taxon A and B share a more recent common ancestor with each other than either shares with C. Sister taxa are defined as two lineages that diverge from the same immediate internal node, sharing an MRCA not shared by any other group.
  • Step 3: Rotational symmetry around nodes: Because branch connections represent lineage splits in time, branches can swivel freely 180° around any internal node like a mobile hanging from the ceiling without altering the underlying nested relationships. Reading taxa strictly by their terminal left-to-right order is an evolutionary fallacy; one must trace backwards down the branches to find common ancestral nodes.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) phylogenetic trees do not represent a ladder of progress (scala naturae); all extant species at the tips have been evolving for the exact same amount of time since the root.
  • ✗ (C) unless a tree is explicitly scaled as a phylogram with a designated branch length key (representing time or substitution rate), branch lengths simply show branching topology.
  • ✗ (D) taxonomic nomenclature has no biological relationship to evolutionary topology.
Question 162 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (D) Clades are defined by shared derived characters (synapomorphies)—evolutionary evolutionary novelties unique to a particular clade ...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Cladistic characters: Cladistics distinguishes between two types of homologous traits: 1) Symplesiomorphies (shared ancestral traits): Characters that originated in an ancestor prior to the clade's MRCA (e.g., the presence of a vertebral column when analyzing relationships among mammals). Because all members possess them, ancestral traits provide zero information about branching patterns within the group. 2) Synapomorphies (shared derived traits): Evolutionary novelties that arose in the MRCA of a specific clade (e.g., mammary glands and hair in mammals). Only synapomorphies identify monophyletic clades.
  • Step 2: Maximum Parsimony principle: When analyzing multiple characters across multiple taxa, different characters may suggest conflicting branch arrangements (due to homoplasy from convergence or reversals). The principle of Maximum Parsimony (Occam's razor) states that the most plausible scientific hypothesis is the simplest one.
  • Step 3: Tree selection: In phylogenetics, the most parsimonious tree is the specific branching topology that minimizes the total number of character state transitions (e.g., fewest total base substitutions across all sequence positions) required to explain the character distribution across terminal taxa.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) symplesiomorphies (shared ancestral traits) cannot resolve branching relationships among descendant taxa within a clade.
  • ✗ (B) maximum parsimony seeks to MINIMIZE (not maximize) convergent mutations and homoplasy.
  • ✗ (C) phylogenetic systematics relies on evolutionary characters (morphology, embryology, genomics), not ecological geography alone.

Question 164 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (C) Temporal isolation occurs when closely related species mate at different times of day, seasons, or years (e.g., the eastern spotte...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Classification of reproductive barriers: Reproductive barriers are categorized into prezygotic (preventing mating or fertilization) and postzygotic (operating after hybrid zygote formation).
  • Step 2: Prezygotic barrier types: 1) Temporal isolation: Species breed at different times of day, different seasons, or different years (classic example: Spilogale skunks breeding in winter vs late summer; Magicicada periodical cicadas emerging every 13 vs 17 years). 2) Behavioral isolation: Courtship displays, pheromones, or acoustic signals are species-specific; females will only mate with males performing the exact conspecific ritual (e.g., synchronous flash cadences in fireflies; specific courtship songs in Drosophila). 3) Habitat isolation: Two species occupy different ecological microhabitats in the same general area (e.g., terrestrial garter snakes vs aquatic garter snakes). 4) Mechanical isolation: Morphological incompatibilities prevent copulation ('lock and key' genitalia in insects). 5) Gametic isolation: Sperm cannot survive in female reproductive tract or surface bindin proteins on sperm fail to bind egg vitelline envelope receptors (e.g., red and purple sea urchins spawning into the same water column).
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) breeding in different seasons is temporal isolation, not gametic isolation.
  • ✗ (B) courtship displays and dances represent behavioral isolation, not mechanical isolation.
  • ✗ (D) biochemical incompatibility of sperm and egg receptors is gametic isolation, not habitat isolation.
Question 165 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) The mule receives a haploid set of 32 chromosomes from the mare and a haploid set of 31 chromosomes from the donkey jack, giving i...

  • Step 1: Chromosomal stoichiometry in equine hybrid: The domestic horse egg contributes n = 32 chromosomes. The donkey sperm contributes n = 31 chromosomes. The resulting fertilized hybrid zygote contains 2n = 32 + 31 = 63 chromosomes.
  • Step 2: Somatic viability: Because all 63 chromosomes carry a full complement of mammalian physiological genes, mitotic divisions throughout development proceed smoothly. Sister chromatids separate independently during somatic mitosis, enabling the mule to develop into a vigorous, healthy, and long-lived adult organism (no hybrid inviability).
  • Step 3: Meiotic breakdown in gametogenesis: In meiosis, gametogenesis requires homologous chromosomes to pair up precisely during zygotene/pachytene of Prophase I (synapsis) to form bivalents (tetrads). Because the horse and donkey karyotypes have undergone extensive chromosomal rearrangements (inversions, Robertsonian fusions/fissions), most maternal and paternal chromosomes lack identical homologous partners. Furthermore, the odd chromosome number (63) means at least one chromosome has no partner at all. Unpaired chromosomes trigger the spindle assembly checkpoint or segregate randomly, producing gametes with wildly unbalanced aneuploidy that cannot support embryonic development.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) mules have perfectly functional circulatory and cardiovascular systems.
  • ✗ (C) mules develop normal external and internal gonadal anatomy and produce hormones; they simply produce non-viable gametes.

  • Step 1: Definition of allopatric speciation via vicariance: Allopatric speciation occurs when a physical geographic barrier divides a biological population into two or more disjunct geographic populations, preventing gene flow. Question 167 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (C) Total meiotic or mitotic non-disjunction produces unreduced diploid (2n) gametes; fusion of two unreduced gametes (or chromosome d...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Mechanisms of polyploid formation: Polyploidy (possessing more than two complete sets of chromosomes) is widespread in plant evolution (~70% of angiosperms have polyploid ancestry). 1) Autopolyploidy: An individual receives extra chromosome sets derived from a single species, typically through meiotic non-disjunction generating unreduced 2n gametes that fuse to yield a 4n tetraploid. 2) Allopolyploidy: Two different species hybridize, followed by mitotic or meiotic genome doubling, creating an amphidiploid that possesses homologous pairs for every chromosome.
  • Step 2: Instantaneous reproductive isolation: A tetraploid plant (4n) can produce functional 2n gametes and successfully self-fertilize or cross with other tetraploids. However, if a tetraploid (4n) crosses with an ancestral diploid (2n): 2n gamete (from 4n) + 1n gamete (from 2n) = 3n (triploid) zygote.
  • Step 3: Sterility of triploid hybrids: During Prophase I of meiosis in a triploid, the three sets of chromosomes attempt to pair. Trivalents or univalents form, but they cannot segregate evenly into two daughter cells during Anaphase I. Gametes receive wildly chaotic aneuploid chromosome numbers, resulting in nearly 100% hybrid sterility (the reason seedless watermelons and commercial bananas are triploid!). Because hybridization produces sterile offspring, the tetraploid lineage is instantly reproductively isolated from its sympatric diploid ancestors.

These spatial barriers facilitated repeated allopatric speciation events as small populations hopped from island to island. 3) Divergent natural selection: Natural selection favored beak variations that efficiently exploited distinct food resources: the 'I'iwi evolved a long, sickle-shaped decurved bill to harvest nectar from curved lobeliad corollas, the Maui parrotbill evolved a parrot-like crushing beak to rip open branches for beetle larvae, and the Palila evolved a thick, stout beak to crack tough mamane seeds.

Question 169 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) Phyletic Gradualism posits that species evolve slowly, smoothly, and continuously over millions of years through gradual accumulat...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Darwinian phyletic gradualism: Traditional Darwinian models assumed that morphological divergence proceeds slowly, steadily, and imperceptibly across vast geological expanses, predicting that complete fossil strata should reveal continuous chains of intermediate transitional forms connecting ancestral and descendant species.
  • Step 2: The paleontological reality of stasis: Eldredge and Gould pointed out that real sedimentary sequences rarely show smooth gradual transformation. Instead, paleontologists repeatedly observe that: 1) Most species appear abruptly in a fossil stratum with fully formed novel morphologies; 2) The species persists virtually unchanged for millions of years (morphological stasis); 3) The species disappears abruptly from the record.
  • Step 3: The punctuated equilibrium synthesis: Eldredge and Gould explained that this is not an imperfection of the fossil record, but the true signature of Ernst Mayr's peripatric speciation. When a small subpopulation becomes geographically isolated at the ecological periphery of a large parent population, rapid divergence occurs in a small population over a few thousand years (a blink of an eye in geological time, unlikely to be captured in the fossil record). Once the new species is reproductively isolated and establishes a large population, stabilizing selection maintains stasis for millions of years until extinction. Today, biologists recognize that both gradualism and punctuated equilibrium occur across different evolutionary lineages.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) punctuated equilibrium describes macroevolutionary speciation dynamics, not immortality.
  • ✗ (C) both models are scientific evolutionary frameworks rooted in empirical fossil data, not creationism or statues.
  • ✗ (D) punctuated equilibrium was formulated from studies of fossil mollusks and trilobites, and applies across metazoan clades.

★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (D) Ecological release and explosive adaptive radiation; the elimination of dominant apex dinosaurs vacated countless terrestrial ecol...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: The K-Pg boundary impact: Approximately 66 million years ago, a 10-km diameter carbonaceous chondrite asteroid struck Chicxulub (Yucatán Peninsula). The catastrophic impact triggered global wildfires, mega-tsunamis, acid rain, and injected sulfur aerosols and soot into the stratosphere, blocking sunlight for years ('impact winter') and collapsing marine and terrestrial food webs dependent on photosynthesis.
  • Step 2: Selective survival: Large ectothermic and endothermic non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs, plesiosaurs, and ammonites with high metabolic caloric demands were eliminated. Small, burrowing animals, generalist detritivores, crocodilians, and small nocturnal insectivorous mammals survived in subterranean shelters feeding on seeds and decaying organic matter.
  • Step 3: Macroevolutionary aftermath: Mass extinctions are ecological resets. For over 140 million years, non-avian dinosaurs had monopolized terrestrial megafaunal niches, suppressing mammalian body size and ecological divergence. The sudden extinction of the dinosaurs created immense ecological release—vacating millions of square miles of productive habitats and trophic niches. In the ensuing Paleocene and Eocene epochs, the surviving ancestral mammals underwent an explosive adaptive radiation, diversifying rapidly into apex predators, massive herbivores, swimming whales, and flying bats.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT

  • ✗ (B) reptiles are heterotrophs and cannot perform photosynthesis.

Question 171 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) Kleiber's Law and the Surface-Area-to-Volume (SA:V) ratio; smaller endothermic mammals possess a substantially higher SA:V ratio t...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Distinction between total vs mass-specific metabolic rate: Total metabolic rate scales with body mass to roughly the 3/4 power (BMR ∝ M^0.75, Kleiber's Law). Consequently, an elephant consumes far more total oxygen per hour than a mouse. However, mass-specific metabolic rate (metabolism per unit gram of tissue) scales as M^(-0.25).
  • Step 2: Surface-Area-to-Volume geometry: As an organism increases in size, its volume (and mass) increases with the cube of linear dimensions (r³), while its surface area increases only with the square (r²). A tiny 25-g harvest mouse has a massive surface area relative to its minuscule mass (high SA:V ratio).
  • Step 3: Thermal consequences for endotherms: Heat loss occurs across external body surfaces. Because the mouse loses thermal energy to the environment at a staggering rate per gram of body mass, its cells must burn through glucose and fatty acids at breakneck speeds via mitochondrial aerobic respiration to produce metabolic heat. This requires a resting heart rate of ~600 beats per minute and consuming food equal to its own body weight every few days. The elephant, with its low SA:V ratio, retains heat exceptionally well and possesses a relaxed mass-specific metabolic rate with a resting heart rate of ~30 beats per minute.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) mice are mammals and strictly endothermic; animals cannot absorb ATP from sunlight.
  • ✗ (C) all mammals rely on mitochondria for aerobic ATP generation in muscle tissue.
  • ✗ (D) respirometers measure O2 consumption and CO2 production, not ozone gas.

STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Optimal foraging principles: Natural selection evaluates foraging strategies as an energetic cost-benefit equation: Net Energy Gain = Energy Obtained (calories in food) - Energy Expended (searching, capturing, handling).

In the wild, crows flew to an average height of 5.23 meters, adhering almost perfectly to the energetic optimum dictated by natural selection.

  • ✗ (A) flying to 50 meters wastes enormous flight energy without added benefit, violating optimal foraging.

Question 173 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) Phytochrome exists in two interconvertible photoreversible forms: Pr (absorbs red light at 660 nm and is converted to biologically...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: The phytochrome photoreversible switch: Phytochrome is a homodimeric chromoprotein possessing a tetrapyrrole light-sensing chromophore (phytochromobilin). It exists in two photo-interconvertible states: 1) Pr (inactive form): Absorbs red light (660 nm), which isomerizes the chromophore and converts it into Pfr. 2) Pfr (active form): Absorbs far-red light (730 nm), converting it back to Pr. Sunlight contains a high ratio of red to far-red light (~1.2), so daytime light rapidly converts nearly all phytochrome into active Pfr.
  • Step 2: Dark reversion and night length measurement: In darkness, Pfr either degrades via ubiquitin-proteasome proteolysis or slowly reverts enzymatically back to Pr. By measuring the accumulation of Pr (or the decline of Pfr), the plant measures the duration of continuous darkness.
  • Step 3: Effect of light flashes on short-day plants: Short-day plants require a continuous dark period that exceeds a critical night length to induce the florigen transcription factor CONSTANS/FT. If a long, inductive 14-hour night is interrupted by even a 1-minute flash of red light (660 nm) at hour 7, the flash converts Pr to Pfr. The presence of Pfr tricks the plant into perceiving two short nights (7 hours each), neither of which meets the critical dark threshold, completely aborting flowering.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) red light triggers molecular photoreversible signaling, not root dehydration.
  • ✗ (C) short-day plants require long continuous dark periods, not 24 hours of continuous light.
  • ✗ (D) phytochrome is a photoreceptor kinase/transcription regulator, not a digestive enzyme destroying meristems.

Respiration (R) = Oxygen consumed by aerobic respiration of all organisms in the bottle. Net Primary Productivity (NPP) = Energy/oxygen remaining after cellular respiration: NPP = GPP - R.

  • Step 3: Calculate Net Primary Productivity (NPP) from the Light Bottle: In the light bottle, both photosynthesis and respiration occur simultaneously. The net change in DO represents NPP: NPP = Light Bottle DO - Initial DO = 10.5 mg/L - 8.0 mg/L = +2.5 mg O₂/L produced.

  • ✗ (A) it confuses the raw DO concentrations with metabolic productivity rates.

Question 175 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (C) Approximately 10% (ranging typically between 5% and 20%); according to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, energy transformations ar...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: The 10% ecological rule: Raymond Lindeman's classic work demonstrated that across most ecological food webs, average trophic efficiency is roughly 10% (typically varying between 5% and 20% depending on organismal physiology and assimilation efficiency).
  • Step 2: Accounting for energy loss at each step: When a primary consumer (herbivore) eats plant biomass: 1) Not all biomass is ingested (roots, woody stems, spines are left uneaten). 2) A substantial fraction of ingested food cannot be digested or absorbed and is excreted as feces (unassimilated energy). 3) Of the assimilated energy, the vast majority is oxidized in cellular respiration (glycolysis, citric acid cycle, ETC) to synthesize ATP for muscle contraction, active transport, and cellular repair, ultimately dissipating into the environment as metabolic heat (entropic energy loss required by the Second Law of Thermodynamics). 4) Only the small fraction allocated to somatic tissue growth or reproduction (secondary production) is stored as biomass available to the next trophic level.
  • Step 3: Ecological limit on food chain length: If primary producers produce 10,000 joules: Primary consumers receive ~1,000 J; Secondary consumers receive ~100 J; Tertiary consumers receive ~10 J; Quaternary consumers receive ~1 J. There simply is not enough remaining usable energy to support viable populations of top predators beyond the 4th or 5th trophic level.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) while total energy is conserved (First Law), usable free energy declines and degrades into non-reusable metabolic heat (Second Law).
  • ✗ (B) trophic transfer is far lower than 50%, and metabolic heat radiates locally, not being absorbed by ozone.
  • ✗ (D) animals do not produce nuclear radiation from ingested food.
Question 176 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT

STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: The paradox of the inverted biomass pyramid: If you take a snapshot of a cubic meter of open ocean water, you might weigh 4 grams of microscopic phytoplankton (unicellular diatoms and dinoflagellates) and 21 grams of zooplankton (copepods, krill). A biomass snapshot shows an inverted pyramid (higher herbivore biomass).
  • Step 2: Resolution through turnover time: Biomass is a static static measurement of standing crop (mass/area at one instant in time), whereas energy is a dynamic flux rate (energy/area/time).
  • Step 3: High turnover rate: Unicellular phytoplankton have zero non-photosynthetic woody structural tissue (unlike forest trees whose biomass consists of centuries-old inert lignin and cellulose). Phytoplankton divide rapidly (turnover time of a few days or hours). As fast as new phytoplankton cells are born, they are consumed by zooplankton. Thus, a tiny standing crop of phytoplankton produces a staggering total amount of chemical energy over time. The pyramid of energy (productivity in Joules/m²/year) is strictly upright and broad at the base, fully satisfying the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) zooplankton are heterotrophs that actively graze on phytoplankton.
  • ✗ (B) phytoplankton rely on normal chlorophyll-driven sunlight absorption, not dark matter.
  • ✗ (C) a pyramid of energy can NEVER be inverted in any stable ecosystem due to the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
Question 177 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (A) Biological Nitrogen Fixation: Diazotrophic bacteria (such as mutualistic Rhizobium in legume root nodules, or free-living Azotobac...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Nitrogen Fixation: The N≡N triple bond requires 945 kJ/mol to break. Only prokaryotes possessing the molybdenum-iron enzyme Nitrogenase can catalyze the reduction: N₂ + 8 H⁺ + 8 e⁻ + 16 ATP → 2 NH₃ + H₂ + 16 ADP + 16 Pi. Because nitrogenase is irreversibly inactivated by O₂, diazotrophs protect it using leghemoglobin (in legume nodules) or thick heterocyst walls (in cyanobacteria like Anabaena).
  • Step 2: Nitrification: Chemoautotrophic nitrifying bacteria in the soil oxidize reduced nitrogen compounds to harvest electrons for ATP synthesis: 1) Ammonia oxidation: Nitrosomonas oxidizes NH₄⁺ to nitrite (NO₂⁻). 2) Nitrite oxidation: Nitrobacter oxidizes NO₂⁻ to nitrate (NO₃⁻). Plants readily assimilate nitrate through root proton-coupled symporters into glutamate and nucleic acids.
  • Step 3: Ammonification and Denitrification: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down organic nitrogen from dead biomass into NH₄⁺ (ammonification). Under anaerobic conditions (such as waterlogged soils or hypoxic marine sediments), denitrifying bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas stutzeri) use nitrate (NO₃⁻) as a terminal electron acceptor in anaerobic respiration, reducing it sequentially to NO, N₂O, and finally back to inert atmospheric N₂ gas, completing the global cycle.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) nitrogen fixation is carried out exclusively by prokaryotes with nitrogenase, not multicellular earthworms.
  • ✗ (C) denitrification is performed by anaerobic bacteria, not plant chloroplasts.
  • ✗ (D) natural biological and lightning nitrogen fixation have driven terrestrial biosphere cycles for billions of years.

Question 178 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (C) Phosphorus enters ecosystems solely through the slow geological weathering of phosphate-bearing rocks (apatite) into dissolved ort...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Geological nature of phosphorus: Phosphorus has no stable gaseous state under ambient planetary conditions (it does not circulate as a gas in the atmosphere). Its major reservoir is the lithosphere (sedimentary rock deposits). Natural weathering of rock by rain and wind releases dissolved inorganic orthophosphate ions (PO₄³⁻ and HPO₄²⁻) into soil and water at an extremely slow geological pace.
  • Step 2: Limiting nutrient status: Phosphorus is an essential component of nucleic acids (DNA/RNA backbones), phospholipids (cell membranes), and ATP. Because it is released so slowly and binds tightly to iron, aluminum, and calcium in soil, biologically available phosphorus is typically the primary limiting nutrient for primary productivity in freshwater lakes and rivers (as demonstrated by David Schindler's whole-lake experiments).
  • Step 3: Cultural eutrophication cascade: 1) Runoff of agricultural fertilizers, livestock manure, and untreated sewage injects concentrated phosphate into waterways. 2) Removal of the limiting nutrient triggers an explosive population boom of algae and cyanobacteria (algal bloom). 3) The dense surface bloom blocks sunlight, killing submerged aquatic vegetation. 4) As the short-lived algal bloom dies, enormous quantities of dead organic matter sink. 5) Heterotrophic aerobic bacteria decompose the dead biomass, consuming vast amounts of dissolved O₂ in cellular respiration. 6) Dissolved oxygen plummets below critical survival thresholds (<2 mg/L), resulting in widespread hypoxic fish kills and catastrophic biodiversity collapse.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) phosphorus does not have a gaseous atmospheric phase under biological conditions.
  • ✗ (B) biological bioluminescence uses luciferase enzymes and ATP/luciferin, not toxic elemental white phosphorus.
  • ✗ (D) eutrophication is an ecological phenomenon of nutrient pollution and microbial hypoxia, not rock solidification.
Question 179 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) CO₂ reacts with water to form carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which dissociates into hydrogen ions (H⁺) and bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻); the excess...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Equilibrium chemistry of marine CO2 absorption: 1) Atmospheric CO2 dissolves in surface seawater: CO₂ (aq) + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid). 2) Carbonic acid rapidly dissociates into a proton and bicarbonate: H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. The surge in free H⁺ ions has driven average ocean surface pH down from 8.21 to 8.10 (a ~30% increase in hydrogen ion concentration, as pH is on a logarithmic scale).
  • Step 2: Carbonate ion depletion: The excess free H⁺ ions react with existing free carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) dissolved in seawater: H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ ⇌ HCO₃⁻.
  • Step 3: Biological impact on calcification: Calcifying marine organisms—including scleractinian reef-building corals, pteropods (pelagic sea butterflies), foraminifera, and bivalves (clams, oysters)—build their hard external structures by combining calcium ions with carbonate ions: Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ ⇌ CaCO₃ (aragonite or calcite). By scavenging free carbonate ions into bicarbonate, ocean acidification lowers the carbonate saturation state (Omega). This makes it energetically costly or impossible for organisms to precipitate CaCO₃, and can even cause existing calcium carbonate structures to chemically dissolve.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) ocean acidification forms weak carbonic acid, not hydrochloric acid, and does not dissolve whale skeletons (whales have calcium phosphate bones).
  • ✗ (C) adding CO2 LOWERS pH (makes water more acidic), rather than increasing it to alkaline pH 14.
  • ✗ (D) biological photosynthesis fixes carbon into organic carbohydrates, never producing uranium.
Question 180 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (D) When the product of the coefficient of relatedness (r, the fraction of genes shared between actor and recipient by common descent)...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: The evolutionary problem of altruism: At first glance, natural selection appears to disfavor any behavior that lowers an individual's own reproductive success to benefit another individual.
  • Step 2: Hamilton's Rule formulation: W. D. Hamilton recognized that alleles can propagate into future generations not only through an individual's direct offspring (direct fitness), but also by helping genetic relatives who share identical copies of those alleles survive and reproduce (indirect fitness). The sum of direct and indirect fitness is an individual's inclusive fitness.
  • Step 3: The mathematical inequality: Hamilton's Rule states that natural selection will favor an altruistic gene whenever: rB > C, where: 1) r = coefficient of relatedness (probability that a gene in the actor is identical by descent to a gene in the recipient: r = 0.5 for siblings/parents, r = 0.25 for half-siblings/nieces/nephews, r = 0.125 for first cousins); 2) B = reproductive benefit to the recipient (extra offspring produced because of the help); 3) C = reproductive cost to the actor (offspring the actor loses by performing the behavior).
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) if r = 0, then rB = 0, which can never exceed positive cost C (cannot evolve via kin selection).
  • ✗ (B) if cost C exceeds rB, the behavior reduces inclusive fitness and will be eliminated by selection.
  • ✗ (C) cannibalism is not kin-directed altruism.

Question 181 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (B) Clumped dispersion (the most common in nature) arises from patchy resource distribution, microhabitat preferences, or social group...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Clumped (aggregated) dispersion: The most prevalent pattern in the natural world. Driven by heterogeneous environmental factors where vital resources (water holes, nutrient-rich soil patches, cover) are localized, or by social structures (cooperative foraging packs, mating swarms, predator defense herds).
  • Step 2: Uniform (regular/spaced) dispersion: Results from direct antagonistic or repelling interactions between individuals that maintain a minimum distance from neighbors. In animals, it is frequently driven by territoriality (e.g., gannets nesting on cliffs maintain pecking distance). In plants, it is driven by intense competition for scarce soil moisture or root allelopathy (e.g., creosote bushes secreting secondary metabolites that suppress nearby germination).
  • Step 3: Random dispersion: Unpredictable spacing that occurs only when physical and chemical factors are relatively homogeneous across the landscape, and individuals do not exert strong positive or negative social/competitive forces on one another. An example is wind-blown dandelion seeds germinating opportunistically wherever they land across a grassy pasture.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) clumped dispersion is the normal, baseline state driven by patchy resources and sociality, not rare volcanic flight.
  • ✗ (C) uniform dispersion is maintained by behavioral territorial spacing or root chemical inhibition, not physical explosions.
  • ✗ (D) random dispersion is an ecological field phenomenon found in natural wild plant communities.

★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (D) 400 fish
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: The Lincoln-Petersen mark-recapture formula: The method assumes that the proportion of marked individuals in the second recapture sample equals the proportion of marked individuals in the entire lake population: m / n = M / N, which rearranges to: N = (M × n) / m.
  • Step 2: Define the variables from the problem: 1) M = Number of individuals caught, marked, and released in the first sample = 80 fish. 2) n = Total number of individuals caught in the second sample = 100 fish. 3) m = Number of marked individuals recaptured in the second sample = 20 fish.
  • Step 3: Calculate total population size (N): N = (80 × 100) / 20 = 8,000 / 20 = 400 fish.

  • ✗ (A) 160 would be (80 × 20) / 10, misapplying the algebraic formula.
  • ✗ (B) 200 is half the true estimate.

Question 183 Analysis
★★★★ MANDATORY
Correct Answer: (A) Density-dependent: A virulent fungal respiratory pathogen spreads rapidly through a crowded prairie dog town, where high populatio...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Density-dependent factors: A limiting factor is density-dependent if its per capita effect on birth rates or death rates changes as population density changes (usually imposing negative feedback that increases per capita mortality or decreases per capita natality as density rises). Examples include intraspecific competition for food/nesting territory, accumulation of toxic metabolic wastes, predation pressure (predators focus on abundant prey), and transmission of contagious infectious diseases/parasites.
  • Step 2: Density-independent factors: A limiting factor is density-independent if its per capita impact on mortality or reproduction is completely unrelated to population density (exerting the same percentage toll regardless of crowding). Examples are abiotic climatic events and natural disasters: flash floods, freezes, droughts, wildfires, hurricanes, and volcanic eruptions.
  • Step 3: Verification of options: In (A), disease transmission intensifies as host proximity increases (density-dependent), whereas a catastrophic flood destroys a fixed percentage of individuals by drowning regardless of density (density-independent).
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (B) earthquakes are abiotic density-independent disasters, and competition for grass is density-dependent (the reverse of the statement).
  • ✗ (C) both types of regulatory factors operate across all terrestrial and aquatic biomes.
  • ✗ (D) density-dependent factors provide negative feedback that slows growth toward carrying capacity, not driving unchecked exponential growth.

ANSWER SECTION SOLUTIONS Q184 – Q186
Question 184 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (C) The per capita growth rate (rₘₐₓ) remains constant, but the absolute number of individuals added per unit time (dN/dt) accelerates...
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Mathematical formulation of exponential growth: The rate of population growth is given by the differential equation: dN/dt = rₘₐₓ · N, where rₘₐₓ is the intrinsic per capita rate of increase (birth rate minus death rate under ideal conditions) and N is the population size.
  • Step 2: J-shaped trajectory: Although rₘₐₓ is a constant percentage rate per individual, because it multiplies an ever-expanding base population N, each generation adds progressively more individuals than the previous generation (geometric progression: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...). Plotting N against time yields a steep, accelerating J-shaped curve.
  • Step 3: Ecological reality: Exponential growth represents an unconstrained potential. In nature, real populations exhibit exponential growth only temporarily—such as African elephants in Kruger National Park after hunting was outlawed, bacteria inoculating fresh nutrient broth, or invasive species colonizing a new continent. Eventually, density-dependent limiting factors (food depletion, territorial limits, waste accumulation) inevitably intervene.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) exponential growth increases rapidly over time rather than halving.
  • ✗ (B) a horizontal line represents zero population growth (dN/dt = 0), not exponential growth.
  • ✗ (D) exponential growth occurs across many eukaryotic and prokaryotic species under ideal conditions.
Question 185 Analysis
★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
Correct Answer: (B) When N = K / 2 (at exactly half of the carrying capacity, corresponding to the inflection point of the sigmoid curve)
STEP-BY-STEP SOLUTION
  • Step 1: Inspect the logistic differential equation: dN/dt = rₘₐₓ · N · [(K - N) / K]. This equation is a quadratic function of N: f(N) = rₘₐₓ · N - (rₘₐₓ / K) · N².
  • Step 2: Find the maximum by calculus: Taking the derivative of dN/dt with respect to N and setting it equal to zero: d/dN (dN/dt) = rₘₐₓ - 2(rₘₐₓ / K) · N = 0. Solving for N: rₘₐₓ = 2(rₘₐₓ / K) · N ==> 1 = (2/K) · N ==> N = K / 2.
  • Step 3: Biological interpretation: 1) When N is very small (N close to 0): Resources are plentiful, so per capita growth is near rₘₐₓ, but because N is tiny, few total individuals are added per unit time. 2) When N approaches K: The term (K - N)/K approaches zero; density-dependent resistance (starvation, crowding) halts reproduction, so dN/dt approaches zero. 3) At N = K / 2 (the inflection point of the S-shaped sigmoid curve): There is an optimal balance between a substantial number of breeding individuals (N) and low environmental resistance (half the resources still available). This is the point of Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) harvested by wildlife managers.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE INCORRECT
  • ✗ (A) when N = 0, zero individuals are added (dN/dt = 0).
  • ✗ (C) when N = K, (K - K)/K = 0, so population growth completely ceases (dN/dt = 0).
  • ✗ (D) when N > K, the term (K - N) becomes negative, causing population decline (dN/dt < 0), not maximum positive growth.
