FRQ 28: Non-Mendelian Genetics - Incomplete Dominance, Codominance, and Epistasis Official Model Solution ★★★★ MANDATORY
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Incomplete dominance occurs when neither allele is completely dominant, resulting in an intermediate heterozygote phenotype.
• In horses, the C allele produces a normal, full dose of melanin-synthesizing enzyme, while Cᶜʳ produces an inactive enzyme.
• Heterozygotes (CCᶜʳ) produce approximately 50% of normal melanin pigment—an intermediate dilution that lightens a red chestnut coat into golden palomino. Homozygotes (CᶜʳCᶜʳ) produce near-zero pigment, yielding cremello.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Cross: CCᶜʳ × CCᶜʳ
• Genotypic ratio: 1/4 CC : 1/2 CCᶜʳ : 1/4 CᶜʳCᶜʳ (1:2:1 ratio).
• Phenotypic ratio: 1 Chestnut (CC) : 2 Palomino (CCᶜʳ) : 1 Cremello (CᶜʳCᶜʳ) (1:2:1 phenotypic ratio, matching genotypic ratio).
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Cross: Tt × Tt yields 1/4 TT, 1/2 Tt, and 1/4 tt.
• Because homozygous dominant TT is embryonic lethal, TT embryos die prior to birth and are never counted among living offspring.
• The surviving living progeny consist of 2/3 Short-tailed (Tt) and 1/3 Long-tailed (tt), producing a modified 2:1 phenotypic ratio rather than the standard 3:1 ratio.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Epistasis definition: A non-allelic interaction where the phenotypic expression of a gene at one locus alters, masks, or suppresses the phenotypic expression of a gene at a second independent locus.
• Contrast: In standard dihybrid crosses (9:3:3:1), both genes act independently, producing 4 distinct phenotypes. In recessive epistasis (such as Labrador coat color B_E_ [black], bbE_ [chocolate], and __ee [yellow]), the homozygous recessive 'ee' genotype prevents eumelanin pigment deposition, masking the B/b locus entirely. The 3 B_ee and 1 bbee classes collapse into a single yellow phenotype (3 + 1 = 4), transforming the 9:3:3:1 ratio into a 9:3:4 ratio.

Part (A): Exemplary Model Response

- Red eyes, vestigial wings (46 flies)
- Cinnabar eyes, normal wings (44 flies)
Total recombinants = 46 + 44 = 90 flies.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Recombination frequency formula:
RF = (Total Recombinant Offspring / Total Offspring) × 100%
RF = (90 / 1,000) × 100% = 9.0%.
• Genetic map distance:
By definition, 1% recombination frequency = 1 map unit = 1 centimorgan (cM).
Therefore, the genetic distance between cn and vg is 9.0 cM.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response

- cn to vg = 9.0 cM
- b to cn = 9.0 cM
- b to vg = 18.0 cM
• Analysis of additivity: Distance(b to vg) = Distance(b to cn) + Distance(cn to vg) = 9.0 cM + 9.0 cM = 18.0 cM.
• Linear gene order: b — cn — vg (with cn located in the middle, 9 cM from b and 9 cM from vg).
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• In meiotic Prophase I, each crossover event involves only two of the four non-sister chromatids in a bivalent, yielding 50% recombinant and 50% non-recombinant chromatids per single crossover.
• For distant genes (>50 cM apart), multiple crossovers (double, triple, quadruple crossovers) occur frequently. Across all possible multi-strand crossovers, odd crossovers produce recombinants and even crossovers restore parental combinations, averaging out to an asymptotic ceiling of exactly 50% recombinant chromatids.
• Consequently, genes separated by >50 cM assort independently, producing 1:1:1:1 testcross proportions indistinguishable from unlinked genes on different chromosomes.

- Father II-4 is normal (X^D Y).
- If mother II-1 is a carrier (X^D X^d × X^D Y), the probability of having a son with DMD (X^d Y) is 1/4 across all pregnancies (or 1/2 among male offspring).

• Hallmark 2: Zero father-to-son transmission; an affected father passes his Y chromosome to all sons and his single X chromosome to all daughters, meaning sons of affected males never inherit the condition from their fathers, while all daughters of affected males are obligate carriers ('criss-cross inheritance').

FRQ 31: DNA Replication - Asymmetric Replisome Machinery at the Replication Fork Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• DNA Helicase (DnaB): Utilizes ATP hydrolysis to translocate along the DNA strand, breaking hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs to melt the double helix and advance the replication fork.
• Single-Stranded DNA-Binding Proteins (SSBs): Bind cooperatively to exposed single-stranded template DNA to prevent re-annealing and prevent secondary hairpin loop formation.
• Topoisomerase (Gyrase): Relieves positive torsional strain and prevents catastrophic superhelical overwinding ahead of the fork by transiently cleaving phosphodiester bonds, allowing DNA to swivel, and re-ligating the backbone.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• The two parental template strands run antiparallel (one 3' → 5' toward the fork, the other 5' → 3').
• Because DNA polymerases can add nucleotides only to the free 3'-OH end of an existing strand (synthesizing strictly 5' → 3'):
- Leading strand: Synthesized continuously in the 5' → 3' direction toward the advancing fork, requiring only a single initial primer.
- Lagging strand: Synthesized discontinuously in the 5' → 3' direction away from the advancing fork as a series of short segments called Okazaki fragments (1,000-2,000 nt in bacteria, 100-200 nt in eukaryotes), each requiring its own RNA primer.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Step 1 (Primer degradation): Replicative DNA Polymerase III finishes the Okazaki fragment and dissociates. DNA Polymerase I binds to the nick and uses its unique 5' → 3' exonuclease activity to degrade ribonucleotides of the RNA primer one by one.
• Step 2 (Gap filling): Simultaneously, DNA Polymerase I uses its 5' → 3' polymerase activity to add complementary deoxyribonucleotides to the 3'-OH of the upstream fragment (nick translation).
• Step 3 (Ligation): DNA Ligase uses ATP (or NAD⁺) to catalyze the formation of a covalent phosphodiester bond between the 3'-OH of the newly synthesized fragment and the 5'-monophosphate of the downstream fragment, sealing the nick.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: Newly synthesized DNA will consist of fragmented, discontinuous short DNA pieces on the lagging strand, and replication fork collapse or double-strand breaks will occur, halting cell division and causing cell death.
• Mechanism: Without functional DNA Ligase, Okazaki fragments are synthesized and primers are replaced by Pol I, but the final phosphodiester nicks cannot be covalently sealed. The lagging strand remains a collection of detached, broken DNA segments that cannot support chromosome segregation or transcription.
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points

Part (D) Predicts fragmented lagging strand DNA / failure of replication / cell death. 1 pt

FRQ 32: Replication - The End-Replication Problem and Telomerase Biology in Cancer Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Cause: DNA polymerases require a pre-existing 3'-OH primer terminus to initiate synthesis and polymerize strictly in the 5' → 3' direction.
• Lagging strand impact: At the extreme 5' terminus of the newly synthesized lagging strand, an RNA primer was laid down to start the final Okazaki fragment. When this terminal primer is excised by 5' → 3' exonucleases, there is no upstream 3'-OH available for a DNA polymerase to fill the gap. Consequently, a single-stranded 3' overhang remains on the parental template, and the newly synthesized strand is shorter by 50-200 base pairs each cycle.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Repetitive sequence: Human telomeres consist of tandem non-coding hexanucleotide repeats: 5'-TTAGGG-3' (spanning 5 to 15 kilobases in healthy cells).
• Protective cap: The single-stranded 3' G-rich overhang loops back to invade the double-stranded telomere (forming a T-loop) and is bound by a six-protein complex called Shelterin (including TRF1, TRF2, and POT1), which caps the chromosome end to prevent it from being recognized as a broken DNA double-strand break by ATM/p53 repair sensors.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Composition: Telomerase is a specialized ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase composed of: 1) TERC (hTR): an integral non-coding RNA component containing a template sequence (3'-AAUCCC-5'), and 2) TERT: the catalytic protein subunit possessing reverse transcriptase activity.
• Mechanism: Telomerase anneals its internal TERC template to the protruding 3' telomeric overhang and uses its TERT subunit to reverse-transcribe new 5'-TTAGGG-3' repeats in the 5' → 3' direction, extending the parental template strand so conventional primase/polymerase can complete lagging-strand synthesis.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Cancer hallmark: Normal somatic cells lack telomerase; with each division, telomeres shorten until reaching the Hayflick limit, triggering p53-dependent senescence or crisis. Reactivation of telomerase allows cancer cells to maintain telomere length indefinitely, conferring replicative immortality (unlimited proliferation).
• Therapeutic prediction: A TERT inhibitor will cause tumor cells to undergo progressive telomere erosion with each subsequent mitotic division; after several generations, critically uncapped telomeres will trigger DNA damage responses, driving senescence or apoptosis and halting tumor growth.

FRQ 33: Transcription - Eukaryotic Pre-mRNA Processing and Alternative Splicing Mechanisms Official Model Solution ★★★★ MANDATORY
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• 5' Cap: A 7-methylguanosine (m⁷G) cap linked via an atypical 5'-to-5' triphosphate bridge. Functions: 1) protects the transcript against 5' → 3' exonucleases, 2) facilitates nuclear export via CBC, and 3) serves as the binding recognition site for eukaryotic initiation factor eIF4E to recruit the 40S ribosome.
• 3' Poly-A tail: A non-templated stretch of 150-250 adenine residues added following cleavage downstream of AAUAAA. Functions: 1) protects against 3' deadenylation, 2) promotes nuclear export, and 3) circularizes mRNA via PABP-eIF4G interaction to enhance translation efficiency.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Splicing mechanism: Catalyzed by snRNPs (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6).
- The 5' splice donor site contains a conserved 5'-GU-3', the 3' splice acceptor contains 5'-AG-3', and an internal branch-point contains an invariant adenosine.
- First transesterification: The 2'-OH group of the branch-point adenosine mounts a nucleophilic attack on the 5' splice site, cleaving the 5' exon-intron boundary and forming an unusual 2'-5' phosphodiester bond, generating a lariat-shaped intron.
- Second transesterification: The liberated 3'-OH of the 5' exon attacks the 3' splice site, joining exons together and releasing the lariat intron for degradation.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Alternative splicing: By including or excluding specific alternative exons, utilizing alternative 5' or 3' splice sites, or retaining specific introns, different cell types generate different combinations of coding exons from the same primary pre-mRNA.
• In skeletal muscle, specific tropomyosin exons are retained to produce an isoform that binds troponin for fast contraction, while in smooth muscle or fibroblasts, alternative exons are spliced in to optimize actin-binding kinetics for cytoskeletal tension.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: Splicing of intron 3 will fail, resulting in either complete intron retention in the mature mRNA or activation of an aberrant cryptic splice site, causing severe beta-thalassemia.
• Mechanism: The 5'-GU dinucleotide is an obligate, invariant recognition sequence required for base-pairing with the U1 snRNA. Mutating GU prevents U1 snRNP binding. The spliceosome cannot recognize the boundary, leaving the non-coding intron in the mature mRNA. Intron translation introduces premature in-frame stop codons, producing a truncated, non-functional beta-globin polypeptide.

FRQ 34: Translation - Genetic Code Degeneracy, Wobble Hypothesis, and Ribosomal Peptidyl Transfer Official Model Solution ★★★★ MANDATORY
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Redundant (degenerate): Multiple different triplet codons can specify the same single amino acid (e.g., leucine is specified by 6 different codons: UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG).
• Unambiguous: Each individual triplet codon specifies only one and only one specific amino acid (e.g., UUU specifies strictly phenylalanine and never any other amino acid).
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• The first two bases of an mRNA codon pair strictly with the third and second bases of the tRNA anticodon according to Watson-Crick rules.
• At the third base of the codon (the 3' end) and the complementary first base of the anticodon (the 5' end), steric constraints are relaxed ('wobble'). Non-standard hydrogen bonding is permitted (e.g., G can pair with U or C; inosine can pair with U, C, or A). This allows ~45 tRNA species to decode all 61 sense codons accurately.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Ribosomal sites:
- A (aminoacyl) site: Binds incoming charged aminoacyl-tRNA.
- P (peptidyl) site: Holds the tRNA linked to the growing nascent polypeptide chain.
- E (exit) site: Binds deacylated uncharged tRNA prior to release.
• Peptidyl transferase: The 23S/28S rRNA ribozyme catalyzes nucleophilic attack by the alpha-amino group of the A-site amino acid on the ester carbonyl of the P-site peptidyl-tRNA, transferring the peptide chain to the A-site tRNA.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: Ribosomes will translate past UAG stop codons, inserting tyrosine and producing abnormally extended, read-through polypeptides that fail to terminate at normal stop sites.
• Mechanism: The mutated tRNA^Tyr has anticodon 5'-CUA-3', which is complementary to the amber stop codon 5'-UAG-3' (antiparallel 3'-AUC-5'). The mutant tRNA competes with translation release factors (RF1) at the A site, suppressing termination by inserting tyrosine instead of terminating, leading to global read-through errors.

Part (C) Describes A site (incoming aa-tRNA), P site (peptidyl-tRNA), and E site (uncharged exit). 1 pt
Part (C) Describes catalytic peptidyl transferase rRNA ribozyme forming the peptide bond. 1 pt

• Condition 3 (Glucose absent, Lactose absent): Zero transcription (CAP is active, but LacI blocks RNA polymerase).
• Condition 4 (Glucose absent, Lactose present): High/maximal transcription (LacI is off, and cAMP-CAP is active, recruiting RNA Pol II maximally).

• Justification: The lacOᶜ operator mutation prevents the LacI repressor from binding the operator. FRQ 36: Regulation of Gene Expression - The Repressible Trp Operon and Attenuation Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• The regulatory gene trpR constitutively expresses an inactive aporepressor.
• When cellular tryptophan is plentiful, tryptophan acts as a corepressor by binding allosterically to TrpR.
• Tryptophan binding alters TrpR's conformation so its DNA-binding motifs dock into the major groove of the trp operator, physically blocking RNA polymerase from initiating transcription.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• The 162-nt leader transcript (trpL) contains a short open reading frame encoding a 14-amino-acid peptide that includes two consecutive tryptophan codons (5'-UGG-UGG-3') in region 1.
• Downstream of region 1 are four complementary RNA segments capable of forming alternative stem-loop secondary structures: region 1 can pair with 2; region 2 can pair with 3; region 3 can pair with 4.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Tryptophan abundant: The translating ribosome rapidly reads past the tandem Trp codons in region 1, covering region 2. This prevents region 2 from pairing with region 3. Region 3 is forced to pair with region 4, forming a stable 3:4 GC-rich stem-loop followed by a poly-U tract (a Rho-independent terminator). This terminator hairpin knocks RNA polymerase off the DNA, attenuating transcription before structural genes are transcribed.
• Tryptophan scarce: The ribosome stalls at the tandem Trp codons in region 1 due to low charged tRNA^Trp. Region 2 remains free to base-pair with region 3, forming a 2:3 antiterminator hairpin. The 3:4 terminator cannot form, allowing RNA polymerase to transcribe the entire operon.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: Attenuation will no longer respond to tryptophan levels; the operon will attenuate whenever alanine is abundant, and will fail to attenuate when alanine is starved, decoupling attenuation from cellular tryptophan demand.
• Mechanism: The ribosome will stall only if charged tRNA^Ala is depleted, sensing alanine rather than tryptophan. If alanine is abundant, the ribosome reads through region 1, forming the 3:4 terminator hairpin and attenuating the trp operon even if the cell is severely starved of tryptophan.

Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Histone acetylation: Histone Acetyltransferases (HATs) transfer acetyl groups to lysine residues on histone tails, neutralizing their positive charge and weakening electrostatic attraction to negatively charged DNA. This opens chromatin into accessible euchromatin, promoting transcription. Histone Deacetylases (HDACs) remove acetyl groups, compacting chromatin into heterochromatin.

• Distal enhancers/LCR contain binding sites for sequence-specific transcription activators.
• Architectural DNA-bending proteins (cohesin, CTCF) loop the intervening 50-kb chromatin fiber, bringing the LCR-bound activators into direct spatial contact with the core promoter.
• The multi-protein Mediator complex docks onto the activators and bridges directly to the general transcription factors and RNA Polymerase II at the promoter, stabilizing pre-initiation complex assembly and stimulating high-level transcription.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Combinatorial control: Expression of a specific gene requires a unique combination of specific transcription factors (activators).
• All human cells possess identical promoter and enhancer DNA sequences. However, during development, different cell lineages express different repertoires of activators: hepatocytes express activators that recognize the albumin enhancer (driving albumin transcription), but lack immunoglobulin activators. B lymphocytes express immunoglobulin activators while lacking albumin activators. Gene activation occurs only when the full set of necessary activators is co-expressed.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: Adult beta-globin gene expression will be severely depressed or completely silenced, resulting in profound beta-thalassemia.

FRQ 38: Mutations and DNA Repair - Molecular Classes of Mutations and Nucleotide Excision Repair Official Model Solution ★★★★ MANDATORY
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Silent mutation: A nucleotide substitution that changes a codon into a synonymous codon encoding the exact same amino acid, resulting in zero change to the polypeptide sequence.
• Missense mutation: A nucleotide substitution that changes a codon so that it specifies a different amino acid, altering the primary structure.
• Nonsense mutation: A nucleotide substitution that converts an amino acid codon into one of the three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA), causing premature translation termination and a truncated polypeptide.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• The genetic code is read in non-overlapping nucleotide triplets. A 1-nucleotide insertion shifts the triplet reading frame for all subsequent downstream codons (a frameshift mutation), completely scrambling the amino acid sequence and almost invariably generating a premature stop codon within a few dozen residues.
• An insertion of 3 nucleotides adds exactly one in-frame codon, adding a single amino acid while keeping all downstream codons in their proper reading frame.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Step 1 (Damage recognition): Protein sensors (XPC or stalled RNA Pol II) detect the bulky helical distortion caused by the thymine dimer.
• Step 2 (Dual incision): TFIIH helicases unwind the local DNA; endonucleases (XPF and XPG) cleave the phosphodiester backbone on both sides of the lesion (dual incision).
• Step 3 (Excision): An oligonucleotide fragment of ~24-30 nucleotides containing the dimer is excised and released.
• Step 4 (Resynthesis and ligation): DNA Polymerase delta/epsilon fills the gap using the undamaged complementary strand as a template, and DNA Ligase seals the remaining nick.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Genetic basis: Inherited autosomal recessive loss-of-function mutations in any of the seven core NER repair genes (XPA through XPG).
• Clinical symptoms: Extreme sensitivity to solar UV radiation, severe sunburns and freckling upon brief sun exposure, corneal scarring, and a >1,000-fold increased risk of fatal cutaneous malignancies (melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma) at an early age.
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points

Part (B) Explains that 1-nt insertion causes a frameshift scrambling all downstream codons, whereas 3-nt insertion adds only 1 aa in-frame. 1 pt

Part (C) Describes excision of the damaged ~24-30 nt fragment, DNA polymerase gap filling, and DNA ligase sealing. 1 pt

FRQ 39: Biotechnology - Gel Electrophoresis and Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) Official Model Solution ★★★★ MANDATORY
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Net charge: The sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA carries a constant negative charge at alkaline buffer pH due to ionized phosphate groups (-1 per nucleotide).
• Direction of migration: In an applied electric field, negatively charged DNA molecules migrate toward the positively charged electrode (the anode, red lead).
• Size separation: Agarose forms a cross-linked polymer mesh with microscopic pores. Smaller DNA fragments experience less frictional drag and migrate faster through the pore matrix, traveling greater distances than larger, unwieldy fragments (log-linear inverse relationship between base-pair size and migration distance).
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Expected RFLP banding patterns:
1. Homozygous normal (HbA/HbA): Displays TWO bands: 175 bp and 201 bp (both cleavage sites are intact).
2. Homozygous sickle cell (HbS/HbS): Displays ONE band: 376 bp (the central cleavage site is lost, leaving a single uncut fragment).
3. Heterozygous carrier (HbA/HbS): Displays THREE bands: 376 bp, 201 bp, and 175 bp (possessing one mutated allele and one wild-type allele).
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Fluorescent dye: Ethidium bromide (or GelRed / SYBR Safe).
• Molecular interaction: Ethidium bromide is a planar aromatic fluorophore that intercalates between adjacent stacked base pairs of the DNA double helix. When illuminated with ultraviolet (UV) light (~300 nm), the intercalated dye absorbs UV energy and fluoresces visible orange-red light (~590 nm), allowing photographic visualization of DNA bands.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: The DNA samples will migrate in the wrong direction—out of the loading wells toward the top of the gel—and run off into the buffer chamber, resulting in complete loss of all samples and an entirely blank gel.
• Physical reason: Reversing the leads places the positive anode behind the wells. Negatively charged DNA will be repelled by the negative cathode and pulled toward the positive anode at the top of the gel.

FRQ 40: Biotechnology - CRISPR-Cas9 Targeted Genome Editing and HDR Gene Therapy Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Components: The Cas9 endonuclease protein complexed with a synthetic single-guide RNA (sgRNA).
• Guide RNA role: The 5' end of the sgRNA contains 20 nucleotides designed to be complementary to the target DNA sequence, directing the Cas9 complex to that precise genomic locus via Watson-Crick base-pairing.
• PAM role: Cas9 must first recognize a conserved Protospacer Adjacent Motif (PAM, 5'-NGG-3' on the non-target strand) on the host DNA. PAM binding triggers local DNA unwinding, allowing the sgRNA to interrogate the target sequence.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Once the sgRNA base-pairs with the target strand, Cas9 uses two distinct nuclease active sites:
- HNH domain: Cleaves the complementary target DNA strand.
- RuvC domain: Cleaves the non-complementary non-target DNA strand.
• Together, they introduce a blunt double-strand break (DSB) precisely 3 base pairs upstream of the PAM motif.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ): An error-prone repair pathway active throughout the cell cycle that ligates broken DNA ends without a template. NHEJ frequently inserts or deletes small numbers of nucleotides (indels). In a coding exon, indels cause frameshift mutations that create premature stop codons, knocking out gene function.
• Homology-Directed Repair (HDR): A high-fidelity repair pathway active during S/G2 phase that utilizes a homologous DNA donor template to copy missing information. By providing an exogenous donor DNA template carrying the wild-type GAG sequence flanked by homologous arms, HDR precisely corrects the single-base sickle mutation without indels.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Fetal hemoglobin (HbF, α₂γ₂) does not contain beta-globin chains and cannot sickle. During normal neonatal development, the zinc-finger transcription factor BCL11A binds to the gamma-globin promoter to silence fetal hemoglobin, switching the infant to adult beta-globin (HbA or HbS).
• By using CRISPR-Cas9 and NHEJ to mutate the erythroid-specific enhancer of BCL11A, BCL11A expression is abolished specifically in red blood cell precursors.
• Without BCL11A repression, gamma-globin transcription is reactivated, allowing cells to produce abundant fetal hemoglobin (HbF). High HbF inhibits HbS polymerization, preventing erythrocyte sickling and curing vaso-occlusive symptoms.

STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Homologous structures are anatomical traits shared by different species because they were inherited from a common ancestor that possessed that ancestral structure.
• The forelimbs of humans (grasping), bats (flying), whales (swimming), and horses (running) share the identical anatomical arrangement of bones: a single proximal humerus, paired radius and ulna, a cluster of carpals, and five metacarpal/phalangeal digits.
• Although modified extensively by divergent natural selection for radically different functions, the shared underlying skeletal blueprint demonstrates descent with modification from an ancient common Devonian tetrapod ancestor.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Homologous structures share common ancestral origin but may differ in function (divergent evolution).
• Analogous structures perform similar biological functions and appear superficially similar, but evolved independently in unrelated lineages that do not share a common ancestor for that trait.
• Evolutionary process: Convergent evolution, where distinct lineages adapt independently to similar ecological niches or physical aerodynamic/hydrodynamic selective pressures (e.g., wings of insects vs wings of birds).
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Embryological homology 1: Pharyngeal arches (pouches/slits); present in all vertebrate embryos, developing into functional gills in fish, and remodeling into the middle ear cavities, Eustachian tubes, and parathyroid glands in adult terrestrial mammals.
• Embryological homology 2: Post-anal muscular tail; present in all early vertebrate embryos, extending beyond the anus, retained in fish and reptiles for propulsion, and reduced to the vestigial coccyx in adult humans.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Molecular clock and phylogenetic congruence: The number of amino acid substitutions in Cytochrome c is directly proportional to the time elapsed since evolutionary divergence from a shared common ancestor.
• Humans and chimpanzees share an extremely recent common ancestor (~6-7 million years ago), showing 0 substitutions. Rhesus monkeys diverged earlier (~25 mya, 1 difference). Horses diverged with early placental mammals (~80 mya, 12 differences). Tuna fish diverged prior to the water-to-land tetrapod transition (~400 mya, 21 differences).
• This molecular sequence divergence perfectly mirrors the chronological branching order established independently by comparative anatomy and the geological fossil record.

FRQ 43: Phylogeny - Cladistics, Character Matrices, and Maximum Parsimony Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Shared ancestral character (symplesiomorphy): A homologous trait that originated in an ancestor prior to the common ancestor of the clade being analyzed (e.g., vertebral column when analyzing relationships within mammals); it provides zero information about branching patterns within that clade.
• Shared derived character (synapomorphy): An evolutionary novelty unique to a particular clade and its common ancestor (e.g., hair in mammals).
• Only synapomorphies are used to define valid monophyletic clades.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• An outgroup is a taxon that is closely related to the group being studied (the ingroup) but branched off prior to the common ancestor of the ingroup.
• Purpose: It establishes the ancestral character polarity (determining which character states are primitive/ancestral [0] versus derived/novel [1]), allowing systematists to root the tree and determine the direction of evolutionary change.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Linear branching sequence:
1. Outgroup branch: Lancelet (lacks all traits)
[Node 1: Evolution of Vertebral Column]
2. Branch: Lamprey
[Node 2: Evolution of Hinged Jaws]
3. Branch: Salmon
[Node 3: Evolution of Four Walking Limbs (Tetrapody)]
4. Branch: Frog
[Node 4: Evolution of Amniotic Egg and Hair]
5. Terminal branch: Leopard.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Principle of Maximum Parsimony (Occam's razor): States that the most plausible scientific hypothesis is the one that requires the fewest evolutionary assumptions or events.
• In phylogenetic tree construction, when multiple tree topologies are possible due to convergent evolution or reversals, maximum parsimony chooses the specific tree topology that requires the fewest total evolutionary character state transitions (e.g., fewest total nucleotide substitutions or trait gains/losses) across the character matrix.

FRQ 44: Speciation - Prezygotic vs. Postzygotic Reproductive Isolation and Allopatry Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Prezygotic mechanisms:
1. Temporal isolation: Species breed at different times of day or seasons (e.g., eastern spotted skunks breed in late winter, while western spotted skunks breed in late summer).
2. Behavioral isolation: Species exhibit distinct, specialized courtship rituals or signals (e.g., male fireflies flash unique species-specific light pulses that only conspecific females recognize).
3. Gametic isolation: Biochemical incompatibility prevents sperm from fertilizing the egg (e.g., surface bindin proteins on purple sea urchin sperm fail to bind egg vitelline receptors of red sea urchins).
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Postzygotic mechanisms:
1. Reduced hybrid viability (inviability): Hybrid zygotes abort during embryonic development or produce frail, sickly offspring that fail to reach reproductive maturity (e.g., hybridization between certain Rana frog species yields embryos that arrest during gastrulation).
2. Reduced hybrid fertility (sterility): Hybrids develop into robust adults but are sterile due to failed meiotic chromosome pairing (e.g., crossing a female horse 2n=64 with a male donkey 2n=62 yields a vigorous but sterile mule 2n=63).
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Four-stage sequence of allopatric speciation:
1. Geographic barrier formation: A physical barrier (mountain range, canyon, rising isthmus) divides an ancestral population into geographically isolated subpopulations.
2. Cessation of gene flow: Physical separation permanently stops genetic exchange between the isolated gene pools.
3. Independent evolutionary divergence: The isolated populations independently accumulate novel mutations, experience divergent natural selection in different habitats, and undergo random genetic drift.
4. Reproductive isolation: Over time, accumulated genetic differences create prezygotic or postzygotic reproductive barriers, so if the populations ever re-encounter each other, they can no longer interbreed.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: Natural selection will actively strengthen and accelerate prezygotic reproductive barriers—a process known as reinforcement—causing hybrid zone width to shrink and complete speciation to finalize.
• Mechanism: Because individuals that mate across species boundaries waste reproductive effort on sterile or inviable hybrid offspring (low fitness), selection strongly favors individuals that mate strictly with conspecifics. Traits that facilitate mate discrimination (courtship songs, plumage colors) diverge rapidly in sympatry.
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points
Part (A) Correctly describes at least two prezygotic barriers with biological examples (temporal, behavioral, habitat, mechanical, gametic). 1 pt
Part (B) Correctly describes two postzygotic barriers with biological examples (hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility, hybrid breakdown). 1 pt
Part (C) Outlines allopatric speciation: geographic barrier → severed gene flow → independent mutation/selection/drift → reproductive isolation. 1 pt
Part (D) Predicts that prezygotic isolating barriers will be strengthened (reinforcement) and hybrid production will decline. 1 pt
Part (D) Explains that natural selection selects against individuals that mate heterospecifically due to the fitness cost of inviable/sterile hybrids. 1 pt
Part (D) Identifies 'reinforcement' as the evolutionary process strengthening mate discrimination. 1 pt

FRQ 45: Modes of Speciation - Polyploid Sympatric Speciation in Plants Official Model Solution ★★★★ MANDATORY
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Autopolyploidy: An individual receives more than two chromosome sets, all derived from a single species, typically through whole-genome doubling or meiotic non-disjunction within a single lineage.
• Allopolyploidy: An individual receives multiple chromosome sets derived from two or more distinct species, resulting from interspecific hybridization followed by mitotic or meiotic genome duplication, creating an amphidiploid.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Meiotic non-disjunction: If all homologous chromosomes fail to separate during Anaphase I, or all sister chromatids fail to separate during Anaphase II, cytokinesis fails to partition the genome. The resulting gametes retain the full diploid chromosome number (unreduced 2n gametes).
• Tetraploid generation: If a plant self-fertilizes or mates with another individual producing unreduced gametes, two 2n gametes fuse (2n + 2n = 4n), producing a tetraploid zygote with four complete sets of chromosomes.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Immediate reproductive isolation:
- If the tetraploid (4n, making 2n gametes) crosses with a diploid parent (2n, making 1n gametes), the resulting hybrid is triploid (3n).
- Triploid plants are virtually 100% sterile: During Prophase I of meiosis, the three sets of homologous chromosomes cannot achieve balanced bivalent synapsis or segregate evenly during Anaphase I. Gametes receive wildly unbalanced, lethal aneuploid chromosome numbers.
- Because mating with the ancestral population yields sterile offspring, the tetraploid lineage is instantly reproductively isolated within the same habitat.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• The gigas effect and evolutionary vigor:
- Doubling or tripling the genome increases nuclear and cellular volume (larger guard cells, larger xylem vessels, larger parenchyma cells), resulting in larger vegetative leaves, thicker stems, larger flowers, and larger seeds/fruits.
- Possessing multiple copies of every gene buffers against deleterious recessive mutations and allows duplicated gene copies to undergo subfunctionalization or neofunctionalization, conferring wider physiological tolerance to drought, cold, and pests.
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points
Part (A) Contrasts autopolyploidy (chromosome sets from one species) with allopolyploidy (sets derived from hybridization between different species). 1 pt
Part (B) Explains non-disjunction yielding unreduced 2n gametes that fuse to produce a 4n tetraploid zygote. 1 pt
Part (C) Explains that crossing 4n with 2n produces sterile triploid (3n) offspring. 1 pt
Part (C) Explains triploid sterility: 3 chromosome sets cannot segregate evenly during meiotic anaphase I, generating lethal aneuploid gametes. 1 pt
Part (D) Explains the gigas effect: increased cell volume leads to larger morphological organs (leaves, flowers, fruits). 1 pt
Part (D) Explains genetic buffering / multiple alleles conferring wider physiological tolerances. 1 pt

FRQ 46: Energy Flow - Trophic Cascades, Productivity, and the 10% Efficiency Rule Official Model Solution ★★★★ MANDATORY
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Photosynthetic efficiency calculation:
Photosynthetic Efficiency = (GPP / Total Solar Irradiance) × 100%
Efficiency = (20,000 kcal/m²/yr / 2,000,000 kcal/m²/yr) × 100% = 0.01 × 100% = 1.0%.
• Primary producers typically convert only ~1% of incident solar radiation into chemical energy.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• NPP formula: NPP = GPP - R_a
NPP = 20,000 kcal/m²/yr - 12,000 kcal/m²/yr = 8,000 kcal/m²/yr.
• Biological meaning: NPP represents the net rate at which autotrophs accumulate chemical energy as organic plant biomass (growth and reproduction) after meeting their own cellular respiration needs. It is the actual caloric energy available to be consumed by herbivores.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Trophic efficiency calculation:
Trophic Efficiency = (Herbivore Production / NPP) × 100%
Efficiency = (800 kcal/m²/yr / 8,000 kcal/m²/yr) × 100% = 0.10 × 100% = 10.0%.
• Explanation of ~10% constraint: The Second Law of Thermodynamics dictates that every energy transfer increases entropy. 1) Not all plant tissue is consumed (woody roots/fibers left behind); 2) Ingested plant material is partially undigested and excreted as feces (unassimilated energy); 3) The vast majority of assimilated energy is oxidized during cellular respiration to synthesize ATP for locomotion and homeostasis, dissipating into the atmosphere as metabolic heat.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Limit on food chain length: Because ~90% of available energy is lost at each successive trophic transfer, available caloric energy declines exponentially across trophic tiers: Producers (8,000 kcal) → Herbivores (800 kcal) → Carnivores (80 kcal) → Apex predators (8 kcal).
• Beyond 4 or 5 trophic levels, the remaining energy flux is too tiny to sustain viable, reproducing populations of top carnivores over an ecologically realistic foraging territory.
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points
Part (A) Correctly calculates photosynthetic efficiency = (20,000 / 2,000,000) × 100% = 1.0%. 1 pt
Part (B) Correctly calculates NPP = 8,000 kcal/m²/yr and explains it represents organic biomass available to herbivores. 1 pt
Part (C) Correctly calculates trophic efficiency = (800 / 8,000) × 100% = 10.0%. 1 pt
Part (C) Explains energetic loss: unconsumed biomass, fecal excretion, and metabolic heat loss during cellular respiration. 1 pt
Part (D) Explains that food chain length is limited to 4-5 levels because 90% energy loss at each step leaves insufficient energy to support viable apex populations. 1 pt
Part (D) Explicitly references the Second Law of Thermodynamics and thermodynamic entropy. 1 pt

FRQ 47: Biogeochemical Cycles - Microbial Nitrogen Transformations and Carbon Sinks Official Model Solution ★★★★ MANDATORY
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• 1. Biological Nitrogen Fixation: Diazotrophic bacteria (symbiotic Rhizobium in legume nodules; free-living Azotobacter and cyanobacteria) use nitrogenase to reduce atmospheric N₂ into bioavailable ammonia (NH₃ / NH₄⁺).
• 2. Nitrification: Two-step chemoautotrophic oxidation: Nitrosomonas oxidizes ammonium to nitrite (NO₂⁻), and Nitrobacter oxidizes nitrite to nitrate (NO₃⁻), the preferred nitrogen form absorbed by plant roots.
• 3. Denitrification: Facultative anaerobic bacteria (such as Pseudomonas) reduce soil nitrate (NO₃⁻) into nitrous oxide (N₂O) and atmospheric N₂ gas under anoxic conditions, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Agricultural fertilizer runoff delivers massive quantities of nitrate into river systems and coastal bays.
• Nitrogen is a limiting nutrient in coastal marine ecosystems; its sudden abundance triggers massive phytoplankton and cyanobacterial blooms.
• When the algal bloom dies, enormous quantities of dead organic matter sink to the seafloor.
• Aerobic bacterial decomposers proliferate and consume dissolved O₂ through cellular respiration to decompose the dead biomass. Dissolved oxygen drops below 2 mg/L (hypoxia), creating a massive 'dead zone' that suffocates fish, crabs, and shrimp.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Long-term carbon reservoirs: 1) Sedimentary carbonate rocks (limestone / CaCO₃ in the crust) and deep marine sediments; 2) Fossil fuel deposits (coal, petroleum, natural gas) locked deep in the lithosphere.
• Dynamic balance: Autotrophic photosynthesis removes atmospheric CO₂ and fixes it into organic carbohydrates, while aerobic cellular respiration by autotrophs and heterotrophs oxidizes organic carbon, releasing CO₂ back into the atmosphere.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: Reef-building corals will exhibit impaired skeletal growth, structural weakening, and chemical dissolution.
• Chemical cascade: Atmospheric CO₂ dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. The excess H⁺ ions lower ocean pH (ocean acidification) and react with free carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) to form additional bicarbonate: H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻. This depletes the pool of carbonate ions needed by corals to precipitate calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) aragonite skeletons.
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points
Part (A) Correctly outlines nitrogen fixation (N₂ → NH₃ via Rhizobium/nitrogenase) and nitrification (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻ via Nitrosomonas/Nitrobacter). 1 pt
Part (A) Correctly outlines denitrification (NO₃⁻ → N₂ via anaerobic Pseudomonas). 1 pt
Part (B) Explains cultural eutrophication: nitrogen runoff causes algal blooms, and bacterial decomposition of dead algae consumes dissolved O₂, creating hypoxic dead zones. 1 pt
Part (C) Identifies two carbon reservoirs (carbonate rocks/limestone and fossil fuels/marine sediments) and explains photosynthesis/respiration balance. 1 pt
Part (D) Predicts coral skeletal weakening/dissolution. 1 pt
Part (D) Explains ocean acidification chemistry: CO₂ forms H₂CO₃, releasing H⁺ that lowers pH and reacts with CO₃²⁻ to deplete carbonate ions. 1 pt

FRQ 48: Population Ecology - Logistic Growth Dynamics, Carrying Capacity, and Life History Trade-Offs Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• When N = 2,000:
dN/dt = 0.20 × 2,000 × [(8,000 - 2,000) / 8,000]
dN/dt = 400 × [6,000 / 8,000] = 400 × 0.75 = 300 seals/year.
• When N = 4,000 (which is K/2):
dN/dt = 0.20 × 4,000 × [(8,000 - 4,000) / 8,000]
dN/dt = 800 × [4,000 / 8,000] = 800 × 0.50 = 400 seals/year.
• Comparison: The population adds 400 seals/year at N = 4,000, which is significantly faster than the 300 seals/year added at N = 2,000.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• The logistic equation is the product of two terms: the breeding population size (N) and the fraction of remaining carrying capacity [(K - N) / K].
• When N is very small (e.g., N = 500), resources are plentiful (fraction is near 1.0), but there are few breeding individuals, so total births are low.
• When N approaches K (e.g., N = 7,900), there are many individuals, but resources are exhausted; the term (K - N)/K approaches 0, driving growth rate to zero.
• At exactly N = K / 2, the mathematical product of N and (K - N)/K is maximized, producing the steepest slope on the sigmoid curve (the inflection point).
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Factor 1 (Food availability): As seal density increases, intraspecific competition for forage fish (herring, salmon) intensifies, reducing maternal nutrition, lowering birth rates, and increasing pup starvation.
• Factor 2 (Haul-out space / Disease): Limited rocky shoreline haul-out space forces seals into crowded contact, increasing stress and accelerating horizontal transmission of infectious pathogens (such as phocine distemper virus).
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Classification: Harbor seals are K-selected (equilibrium species).
• Justification traits:
1. Large adult body size with long generation time and high longevity (~25-30 years);
2. Delayed sexual maturity (4-6 years of age);
3. Low fecundity (females produce only one pup per year) combined with extensive maternal energetic investment (lactation with lipid-rich milk, maternal guarding).
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points
Part (A) Correctly calculates dN/dt = 300 seals/yr at N = 2,000 and 400 seals/yr at N = 4,000. 1 pt
Part (B) Explains that at N = K/2, the product of breeding individuals (N) and available capacity (K-N)/K reaches mathematical maximum (inflection point). 1 pt
Part (B) Explains that growth rate slows as N approaches K because (K-N)/K approaches zero. 1 pt
Part (C) Describes two density-dependent factors (competition for fish prey, limited haul-out space, disease transmission). 1 pt
Part (D) Classifies harbor seals as K-selected. 1 pt
Part (D) Justifies K-selection using three traits: large body size, delayed maturity, single pup litters, or extensive maternal investment. 1 pt

FRQ 49: Community Ecology - Keystone Predators, Trophic Cascades, and Kelp Forest Dynamics Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Definition: A keystone species is a species that has a disproportionately large effect on its natural environment and community biodiversity relative to its abundance or biomass.
• Paine's experiment: Robert Paine removed the predatory ochre sea star (Pisaster ochraceus) from rocky intertidal plots in Washington. In the absence of Pisaster, its preferred prey, the California mussel (Mytilus californianus), outcompeted all other sessile species for space, driving community species richness from 15 species down to a monoculture of 1, proving top-down keystone regulation.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Pristine kelp forest trophic cascade:
- Tier 1 (Apex predator): Sea otters prey heavily on herbivorous sea urchins, keeping urchin population densities low and forcing surviving urchins to remain hidden in rocky crevices.
- Tier 2 (Herbivore): Urchins remain sparse and feed passively on drifting detached kelp fragments rather than live holdfasts.
- Tier 3 (Primary producer): Giant kelp grows vigorously, forming towering underwater kelp forests that provide structural habitat, nursery grounds, and food for hundreds of marine fish, mollusks, and seabirds.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Consequences of otter removal (urchin barren):
- Released from top-down predator control, herbivorous sea urchin populations explode exponentially.
- Swarms of hungry urchins graze destructively across the seafloor, chewing through the structural holdfasts that anchor giant kelp to the rocky substrate.
- Kelp fronds detach and wash away, clear-cutting the underwater forest into a desolate 'urchin barren.' The complex 3D habitat collapses, causing catastrophic biodiversity loss among kelp-associated fish and invertebrates.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Prediction: Giant kelp biomass will collapse precipitously, transforming healthy kelp forests into barren urchin barrens.
• Four-tier trophic cascade mechanism:
- 1. Killer whales predate heavily on sea otters, driving sea otter populations down by >90%.
- 2. With otters decimated, sea urchins are released from predation, experiencing a demographic boom.
- 3. Swarming urchin populations overgraze kelp holdfasts.
- 4. Kelp forest canopy collapses, demonstrating a four-tier top-down trophic cascade (Killer whales [+] → Sea otters [-] → Urchins [+] → Kelp [-]).
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points
Part (A) Defines keystone species (disproportionate impact relative to biomass) and explains Paine's Pisaster removal experiment preventing mussel monoculture. 1 pt
Part (B) Describes the 3-tier cascade: otters suppress urchins, allowing giant kelp to flourish and support high biodiversity. 1 pt
Part (C) Explains otter removal causing urchin population explosion, holdfast overgrazing, and kelp forest collapse into urchin barrens. 1 pt
Part (D) Predicts that giant kelp biomass will collapse / urchin barrens will form. 1 pt
Part (D) Traces the 4-tier cascade: Orcas eat otters → otters decline → urchins proliferate → kelp is decimated. 1 pt
Part (D) Demonstrates complete mastery of community ecology and top-down regulatory dynamics. 1 pt

FRQ 50: Disruptions to Ecosystems - Invasive Species, Biomagnification, and Climate Mismatch Official Model Solution ★★★★★ VERY IMPORTANT
STEP-BY-STEP ANALYTICAL SOLUTION
Part (A): Exemplary Model Response
• Enemy Release Hypothesis: In its native geographic range, a species' population growth is tightly constrained by a co-evolved guild of specialized natural enemies (predators, parasites, herbivores, and pathogens).
• In an introduced novel range, the exotic species leaves its co-evolved specialist enemies behind. Native predators and pathogens in the novel ecosystem do not recognize or feed effectively on the foreign invader. Freed from top-down population regulation, the invader allocates all metabolic energy to rapid vegetative growth and reproduction, outcompeting native species.
Part (B): Exemplary Model Response
• Bioaccumulation: The accumulation of a contaminant within the tissues of a single individual organism over its lifespan because intake rate exceeds metabolic degradation/excretion rate.
• Biomagnification: The progressive increase in contaminant concentration across successive trophic levels of a food web.
• Mechanism for DDT in apex raptors: DDT is chemically persistent, non-biodegradable, and highly lipophilic (fat-soluble), partitioning into adipose tissues. Due to the 10% trophic efficiency rule, an apex predator must consume thousands of times its body weight in prey biomass over its lifetime. While 90% of prey organic carbon and energy is burned off as CO₂ and heat, nearly 100% of the lipophilic DDT is retained, multiplying toxin concentrations up to 10-million-fold in top raptors, where it disrupts calcium-ATPase to cause paper-thin eggshells.
Part (C): Exemplary Model Response
• Phenology: The scientific study of the timing of recurring seasonal biological life-cycle events (e.g., flowering, insect emergence, bird migration) in relation to climatic cues.
• Phenological mismatch: Warmer spring temperatures cause local plants and ectothermic insects to emerge 2-3 weeks earlier in response to thermal cues. Migratory birds wintering in the tropics rely on day length (photoperiod) to trigger migration, arriving on breeding grounds at their traditional calendar date. By the time bird chicks hatch, peak caterpillar biomass has already passed, leading to food scarcity, chick starvation, and population decline.
Part (D): Exemplary Model Response
• Ecological risks:
1. Non-target host switching: The introduced wasp may switch hosts to parasitize native beneficial beetles or endangered insects, causing unintended native extinctions;
2. Interspecific competition / disruption: The wasp could outcompete native parasitoids or alter food web dynamics, becoming an invasive pest itself.
• Safety measure: Conduct rigorous multi-year quarantine host-specificity testing in biosecure laboratories to confirm that the candidate biocontrol agent is an obligate specialist that attacks strictly the target pest and will starve to death in the absence of that host.
Official AP® 6-Point Scoring Criteria & Guidelines
Part & Criterion Scoring Guidelines Points
Part (A) Explains the Enemy Release Hypothesis: loss of co-evolved specialist predators/pathogens allows unchecked population growth. 1 pt
Part (B) Distinguishes bioaccumulation (individual level) from biomagnification (trophic level increase). 1 pt
Part (B) Explains lipophilic persistence and 90% trophic energy loss concentrating DDT into toxic levels in apex predators (causing thin eggshells). 1 pt
Part (C) Defines phenology and explains how climate warming advances insect emergence, decoupling it from photoperiod-timed bird migration (trophic mismatch). 1 pt
Part (D) Identifies two ecological risks of biological control (non-target host attacks / native species disruption). 1 pt
Part (D) Proposes rigorous quarantine host-specificity testing to ensure obligate specialist feeding on the target pest only. 1 pt

APPENDIX FORMULA REFERENCE & SCORE MATRIX
Essential AP Biology Principles & Equations
Core mathematical equations, thermodynamic formulas, and statistical thresholds required on the AP Biology Examination.
  • Water Potential: Ψ = Ψp + Ψs, where Solute Potential Ψs = -iCRT (i = ionization constant, C = molar concentration, R = 0.0831 L·bar/mol·K, T = temperature in Kelvin = 273 + °C).
  • Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium: p + q = 1 (allele frequencies) and p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (genotype frequencies), where p = dominant allele frequency, q = recessive allele frequency.
  • Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit: χ² = Σ [(O − E)² / E], with degrees of freedom df = n − 1. Critical value at p = 0.05 for df = 1 is 3.84; df = 2 is 5.99; df = 3 is 7.82.
  • Primary Productivity: Net Primary Productivity (NPP) = Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) − Respiration Rate (R).
  • Population Growth Models: Exponential: dN/dt = r_max · N; Logistic: dN/dt = r_max · N · [(K − N) / K], where K = environmental carrying capacity.
  • Q10 Temperature Coefficient: Q10 = (k₂ / k₁)^(10 / (T₂ − T₁)), measuring the rate change with a 10°C increase.
